stand part.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Madam Chair, thank you
for the opportunity to take a short call on Part 1. Part 1 amends the Local Electoral Act
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4659
2001. It puts the poll provisions back in in relation to Māori wards. These are the same
provisions that were in place prior to the last Government’s change.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: We can’t hear.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Oh—is that not working? Was it me? Is that better? Hello.
Is that better? Was it better before —was it? Sorry—well, I won’t apologise to that side;
I’ll apologise to this side. [Gestures to Government benches] Sorry.

items.speaker: Shanan Halbert
items.text: What do you have to be like that for?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Oh, I thought I was being kind.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Can we come back to the bill. Come back to
the bill.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: It refers to the Schedule, which deals with transitional
arrangements and deals with some of the postal time frame arrangements as well—which, of
course, is in regard to the extension of the postal voting period for future local government
elections, which, obviously, is an issue that’s going to need to be further dealt with. This
really is simply a fix in relation to the next local elections.
There’s also two tabled amendments from me. Firstly, there’s one which is more
substantive, and that is in relation to requiring councils to make a choice as to whether they
will rescind, disestablish, or have a referendum. So that is requiring councils by 6 December
to make that decision.  There’s a second one, which has a typo that has been picked up. The
word “or” was missing from one of the clauses and is being fixed.

items.speaker: Hon KIERAN McANULTY
items.text: Thank you very much, Madam Chair. It’s a
shame that we only have seven minutes or so until the dinner break, but we are very much
looking forward to diving into this after the dinner break. There is a lot to cover. It may be
a bill of three parts, but they are detailed, and as the Minister has indicated, there is also an
Amendment Paper that is thicker than the original bill. So there is a lot to talk about. Of
course, this has just been tabled. We haven’t had the opportunity to dive into this and
consider it. So we’re looking forward to using the committee of the whole House stage to
have that as our only opportunity.
I was hoping to be able to have a back and forth. We all live in hope. We’ve tried this
on a number of occasions, and it doesn’t happen very often, but I’ll give it a go and we’ll
see how we get on. I’ll start with a very simple question. Would the Minister consider an
amendment to include all wards of local body areas, all wards under local councils, not just
Māori wards—that they be treated the same under the proposals within this bill?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: No, the Government is
not willing to accept that amendment. This bill is in relation to Māori wards, wards based
on race, ethnicity, rather than geography.

items.speaker: Hon KIERAN McANULTY
items.text: So there we have it right off the bat. The
Government is treating the consideration of the establishment of Māori wards differently to
all other wards—probably the most upfront thing the Minister has said in this House, and
we got it right from the get-go, which I appreciate and thank him for. If we actually get to
the nub of the issue now, what the Minister is asking us to consider tonight is a bill that
brings in different provisions for the establishment of Māori wards than any other wards
under local government—urban, rural, whatever. Whatever that community feels would
best serve them, a local council can make that decision. If a local council wants to establish
Māori wards, the Minister is asking us to vote for a bill that would make that process harder.

items.speaker: My next question is
items.text: does the Minister know what institutional racism is?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: The member Kieran
McAnulty’s comments in relation to my last question highlight, I th ink, a difference in
terms of where the Opposition’s position on this is and where the Government’s position
on this issue is. In relation to rural wards or urban wards, where those wards exist,
4660            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
everybody who lives within those wards, regardless of whether they’re on the Māori roll or
the general roll, gets to vote for the person that they choose to represent them as a mayor or
a councillor. In relation to the position that this Government is taking, we’re simply putting
the provisions back to what they were three years ago. This is not going back to 30 years
ago or 40 years ago; this is simply putting it back to what it was three years ago, which is
saying that if a council wishes to make a change and to have a Māori ward—which means
that voters are split into whether or not they are on the general roll or the Māori roll—they
can put that forward, the public can then petition the council for a referendum, and then
voters in that community are able to have their say and make a decision based on whether
or not they would like to. And if the public in that community decides that, yes, they would
like that—as some councils have—they will have the opportunity to have a Māori ward. If
they vote no, there won’t be. The difference is that it divides the people in that community
based on which roll they’re on. An urban ward or a rural ward does not divide the people
in those wards based on what roll they’re on.

items.speaker: Hon KIERAN McANULTY
items.text: Thank you v ery much, Madam Chair. I
appreciate the response from the Minister, but it was unnecessary, because we know what
the motivations of the Government are. We know that they are wanting, regardless of when
the status quo as it is currently was brought in—it was changed to bring it in line with the
establishment of any other wards. And the cute argument about, “Well, some people are on
different rolls; therefore, we want everyone on the same roll” doesn’t wash because we’re
talking about the establishment of a ward, the recognition of a decision of a council.
I do note that the Minister didn’t answer my last question, so I will read out a definition
of institutional racism. It is defined as “policies and practices that exist throughout a
whole society or organisa tion that result in and support a continued unfair advantage to
some people and unfair or harmful treatment of others based on race”. Now, I think the
committee should reflect on that in the few moments that we have before the dinner break,
because I am very interested to hear the Minister’s view as to how what he is proposing
in this bill—that would treat Māori differently to everybody else in the country—does not
fit the definition that I’ve just read out. And I want the Minister to stand up—he may wait
until after the dinner break. By golly, I’ll give him an hour and a half to think about it if
he wants; I don’t care. But I think he owes the country and I think he owes the House an
explanation. Why is he asking us to treat people differently because of race? Why should
Māori go through a harder process than everybody else?
And it’s interesting, isn’t it, that we have just had a pretty significant moment in this
House to reflect on the report that sits on that Table. Riddled and weaved throughout that
report are examples of institutional racism, and for a brief moment this House stood as
one and said, “Never again.” And in the cruellest of cruel ironies, here we are, the very
first item immediately after on the Order Paper, and the Minister is asking us to v ote for
a bill that treats Māori people differently, creates an unfair advantage for non-Māori, and
creates a pathway for communities that have already made their decisions more difficult
and more likely to be reversed.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: The member Kieran
McAnulty made a wrong assertion in terms of the comments he made earlier in relation to
how the provisions passed by the previous Government treated the Māori wards the same
as any other. The reality was that they took away the ability, when councils were putting
forward their representation reviews, for the public to be able to go to the Local Government
Commission and be able to petition or have their concerns raised around that, even through
the Local Government Commission. When councils are establishing a rural ward, people
can lodge a complaint or lodge a submission to the Local Government Commission. Even
that was taken away. So there was no fair treatment under their provisions. What we are
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4661
doing is we’re simply putting it back to what it was before. Where a council is establishing
a rural ward or where they’re establishing a Māori ward, there are provisions and abilities
for the public to have their say. That is a fair principle. It is a principle that we stand on.
And it’s a principle that I will argue throughout this debate. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB
items.text: I have just a brief
question, really, in terms of the underlying policy of this bill, because I was noting that at
Waitangi in 2024, Christopher Luxon said, “I want te ao Māori to thrive. When Māori do
well, we all know it, New Zealand does well.” We, like you, believe in localism and
devolution, not centralisation and control. And it strikes me that at the guts of this bill is a
movement away from devolution of these decisions from local government. In fact, local
governments have the ability to choose, in their local body, whether or not they have Māori
wards, like they have island wards or rural wards. And I was wondering if there’s been a
change in the Government policies and, in fact, now the Government wants centralisation
and control?

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, the time has come for the dinner
break. The committee is suspended and will resume after the dinner break.
Sitting suspended from 6 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, when we suspended for the dinner
break, we were in committee on the Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori
Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Bill. We are debating Part 1, clauses 3 to
17, “Amendments to Local Electoral Act 2001”, and the Schedule.

items.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair.
I did speak before the dinner break and had a question there around localism that the
Minister may want to answer. But I was chatting to my f riend Peeni Henare and we
noticed how complicated the legislation is to read—and there are some flow diagrams in
the documentation before us.
I guess one of the questions I have for the Minister is why he’s required the rescission
of Māori wards decisions unless there’s a poll, because you don’t need a poll to rescind the
Māori ward itself. It would strike me that the status quo is there now, and what we heard
throughout the committee was that—I think, without exception; I think I can say without
exception—local bodies who had instituted Māori wards were not supportive of this
legislation and wanted to keep the Māori wards. But they knew, as Mr McAnulty said, that
if they went to referendum—because of demography both of their constituencies and of the
people who get out and vote—that it would essentially be a veto on Māori wards.

items.speaker: The question is
items.text: why do we only have a referendum if we want a Māori ward? Why is it
that we can rescind them and we don’t need to go to the electorate to change our electoral
system? Now, you can say that it’s just going back; it’s just returning to the status quo ex
ante, but the fact of the matter is that this reform has been put in place and the fact is that it
was working. I mean, this is a classic bit of politics, because there was no problem to fix.
The only people who really didn’t like this were the National Party and the ACT Party. All
of the people on the ground doing the mahi were very happy with it.
So just looking at that flow diagram —and I’m looking at the select committ ee report
on page 16, and it’s got a couple of group one, group twos. Both the councils can choose
to rescind the Māori ward —so make that electoral decision without going to their
constituency—but if they want to keep the Māori ward, they have to have a bi nding poll
at the local election on a yes/no basis. So why is it —get rid of them, you don’t need a
poll; keep them, you do need a poll?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair.
Thank you for the member’s two questions. I apologise, the dinner break interrupted my
4662            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
ability to answer his question around localism prior to the dinner break. And, of course,
as I’ve outlined in my speeches on this issue, that side of the House talks about localism,
but the localism stops at the council table. We’ve actually said localism should flow
through to the voters, the electors, the people who the councillors and the mayor are meant
to represent. And so that’s why  this Government is taking the action in relation to this
bill, and we believe that is consistent with giving local democracy the opportunity for
local communities to have their say.
The second question he asked in regards to the decision to rescind or dis establish
otherwise there will be a referendum, and that is an opportunity for the councils to make
that decision as part of the process. They will be required to have a referendum. If they
do not wish it to go to a referendum, there is a choice that they can make, which is to
rescind or to disestablish, which is simply a choice that they can make in order for them
not to have to have a referendum. The alternative is that there will be a referendum and
the public will ultimately have their say as part of that process.

items.speaker: CELIA WADE -BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair, I’ve got a number of
questions. I’d like to start with asking the Minister to consider—in the briefing to incoming
Minister of Local Government it was pretty clear that the Minister has some responsibility
for Māori-council relationships. I wonder if he could address how putting an effective veto
on the introduction of Māori wards addresses that ministerial responsibility when we can
see that taking us backwards, with an effective veto on Māori wards—it’s acknowledged
by the Department of Internal Affairs, it’s been acknowledged by the vast majority of
mayors and chairs and Māori councillors; so how he thinks he is actually taking that
responsibility seriously.
I also wonder whether he shares the view of at least one of his party colleagues where,
when standing up as tangata Tiriti, that seemed to be some strange view that it was only for
Māori to advocate for Māori rather than actually being an ally and a partner and working
together—tangata Tiriti and tangata whenua. I have to say I hope that the Minister of Local
Government will reflect on that —hopefully—unthought-through little  bit of heckling
yesterday. I do have some more questions, particularly about the competency of local
government to consult, but I will come back, if I may, to those.

items.speaker: Hon PEENI HENARE
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I was thinking
about some of the singling out of Māori in particular in this bill, and today in the House I
want to reflect on a contribution during question time that was quoting the Far North
District Mayor about insulatio n. Well, the Far North District Mayor and that council
presented to the select committee on this particular bill and made it very clear that,
actually, what’s happening in Te Tai Tokerau is already working really well with Māori
wards and the members who a re on that council. So the questions that I have for the
Minister are—one of them might seem pretty straightforward and pretty simple. As I read
through the bill, it’s quite easy to get lost on some of the dates and I’d really like the
Minister to explain why some of those dates were chosen, for the public who are listening
to this debate—and trust me, there is a lot of interest in this debate; it was reflected in the
submissions on this bill.
Of course, that’s been complicated again by the recent local body elections in Tauranga,
which have then changed it and meant that there’s a different rule for them and now there’s
going to be a slightly different rule for the other councils, again. So I think it would be really
good for the Minister to get up in the House here today and spell it out very clearly about
the dates for all of the councils—as well as Tauranga, given their recent election. That’s the
first question.
The second question I have is—as it says here in the bill, the need for notification that
any council that wishes to go towards a referendum must notify the electorate, if you will,
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4663
by a certain date and give a certain period of time. I wonder —and this is an offer to the
Minister, while he might be hell bent on getting rid of Māori wards —if in his exchange
and his commitment to engagement with the community, he might look towards whether
or not notifications in te reo Māori might be accepted; notifications that engage with the
community that this directly affects —whether or not there is any indic ation, because I
don’t see it in this particular bill, to actually reach those who this is impacting the most,
and that is the Māori community. So that’s perhaps an offer there for the Minister, with
his considerations, to enable that kind of engagement, seeing as he’s hell bent on getting
rid of them. And it’s pretty simple; it is talking about whether it’s in te reo Māori, whether
it’s on the marae.
The other challenge with that too, if I think about the great city that the Minister and I
live in, he might recall the recent referendum that was done on Māori wards at the beginning
of this year in Tāmaki Makaurau, and he’ll understand just exactly how hard it was to
engage right across such a big city. You know, when those who aren’t from Auckland think
about Tāmaki Makaurau, they generally think about the city—maybe a little bit out east,
maybe a little bit out south—but they don’t know or realise that it goes almost all the way
to the Kaipara, it goes all the way to the Hunua Ranges, east to west, and it’s a huge area
with very interesting demographics. So I wonder, with respect to the Auckland super-city,
whether or not there might be another engagement plan, and given that they’ve had their
referendum at the beginning of this year, whether or not the Minister is intending for them
to hold one again. That’s a genuine question to the Minister about this particular bill as it
encourages or pushes, gives them an option—I think I heard the Minister’s words in his
contribution after the dinner break—to either rescind or gives them an option to go to a
referendum. So I wonder if the Minister has any plans on that.

items.speaker: Just the final question from me
items.text: when I think about the way that a regional council works
and the way that perhaps the Far North District Council or even the Whangārei council, and
then you’ve got the regional Northland Regional Council—which covers a very, very large
area—I wonder when, as this bill spells out, the time frames with which they must engage,
the time frames within which they must hold their referendum, I wonder if the Minister has
given enough consideration to just the sheer geography and the challenge and the difference
between a regional council and a district —now Whangārei District Council, I get that;
Whangārei’s reasonably small enough, manageable enough, perhaps—

items.speaker: Hūhana Lyndon
items.text: Big—big as, massive.

items.speaker: Hon PEENI HENARE
items.text: —although I’m sure my colleague here, Hūhana Lyndon,
will argue —and she’s right, if you go out to places like where she and I are from —
Pipiwai, Ngātiwai—it’s really hard to get there. But I wonder, just in the final 10 seconds,
if the Minister wouldn’t mind putting his thought and his energy towards answering
those questions.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair, and
I thank the members for their questions. Her Worship asked regarding the briefing to the
incoming Minister, which I received. Of course there’s obligations wit hin the Local
Government Act for local government to engage with Māori; that is in the Local Government
Act. That principle remains; that’s not being changed by this legislation. Questions in regard
to the Treaty obligations: this doesn’t change any Treaty obligations. Ultimately, this is about
the representation arrangements and the ability of local communities to be able to have their
say in relation to those representation arrangements.
There were questions around the dates and the reasoning for that, w hich I think is a
fair question. The issue in regard to Tauranga, of course, is that they were having their
election prior to this bill going through the House. So the issue there is that they won’t
have the opportunity to have, obviously, a referendum at the election next year in 2025
4664            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
because they won’t be having an election next year in 2025. So there’s specific provisions
in relation to Tauranga there, and the decision was made by Cabinet to hold the
referendums at the same time as the next local electio n to ensure that the costs were
reduced for local councils. That means they could hold them at the same time and the
implementation, therefore, comes into effect from 2028. That was the choice that Cabinet
made in relation to the time frames.
In terms of Auckland, there wasn’t a referendum early in the year. The council did
make a decision not to proceed with establishing a Māori ward. They made that decision
in, I think, October or November last year. That was a decision made by the council not
to proceed  with a Māori ward. Then, in terms of referendums and the process of
undertaking a referendum, there’s already good, established protocol in place in relation
to the running of elections through the local government legislation as well, and by timing
it with the local government elections, which means there’s obviously an information
campaign which will go alongside the local government postal ballot. So by doing it
together it reduces cost but it also means that those communication campaigns can be
utilised to do both of these things.

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I have two questions
for the Minister. If I don’t make it to my second question during my contribution, I will need
to come back for a further contribution, because I have two quite specific questions.
The first question actually relates to the topic we’ve just been discussing and the
Minister has respo nded to around the timing —the timing of both a local government
election and the referendum on Māori wards. The particular scenario I want to put to the
Minister—and to have his response, which I think will be helpful for the committee of
the whole House—is a situation where people are running in an election for a Māori ward
and at the same time there is a referendum occurring on whether that Māori ward is
retained or not. We have a situation where people are campaigning, outlaying money, and
putting their lives on hold in order to run for an elected position, which they subsequently
win, but at the same time, through that referendum, the voting public vote to disestablish
that Māori ward.

items.speaker: My question to the Minister is
items.text: what happens in that scenario? Essentially, you have a
person who has been elected, yet the actual role that they have been elected to has been
disestablished. So I’d be interested in the Minister’s comments on that. That’s my first
question. The second question I have for the Minister is in relation to the referendum and
the types of elected roles that can be put forward for a referendum by the public. The
Minister in an earlier contribution noted his views that the voting public should have a
say in their democracy, and I think all members of this House would agree with that. But
I want to particularly reference a situation with Nelson City Council.
Nelson City Council had a representation review that then was put in place for the
2022 election. Prior to the 2022 election, we had one mayor, elected through first past the
post, and we had 12 councillors elected at large, also through first past the post. There
was a representation review undertaken through the council, and the change was made to
have the mayor elected through single transferra ble vote, or STV, and for those 12
positions to be broken up into geographic wards, of which there are two, and a general
ward and a Māori ward. We ended up with a fulsome representation review that not only
added a Māori ward; it changed the voting system  from first past the post to single
transferrable vote and it also changed the wards from being at large for the entire council
through to having a general ward and then geographic wards.
Now, during that representation review, it would be fair to say that  people submitted
in favour of STV and against STV, in favour of general wards and the geographic ward
and against the geographic ward, in favour of a Māori ward and against a Māori ward.
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4665
Now, in the contributions to the select committee from Nelson City c ouncillors, it has
been pointed out: why is only one of those three decisions now being put forward to a
referendum? Where is the democracy in that?
They’re not necessarily opposed to having a referendum but they’ve been very clear.
This particular councillor who I want to mention, the commentary he made in the meeting
at Nelson City Council when this was being discussed was: OK, if we’re going to have a
referendum on the Māori ward, why don’t we have one on the Stoke -Tāhunanui ward,
which was implemented at the same time? Why don’t we have one on the North Nelson
ward, which was implemented at the same time? Why don’t we have one on the general
ward, which was implemented at the same time? And why don’t we have one on the use
of STV as opposed to first pas t the post, which was also implemented at the same time?
Why is the Māori ward being singled out? There are words I know that I can’t use in this
House. If I could, I would.
Those are my two questions. Why is there such inconsistency in the application of a
referendum based on this idea of democracy that the Minister has put forward, which we all
uphold? If you’re going to apply it, apply it to all decisions that sit under the representation
review. That is my proposition to the Minister, because it’s about  consistency and about
making sure—just on the back of the debate we’ve had today—that we’re not singling out
people based on their ethnicity. Because we’ve seen what’s happened in New Zealand when
that happens, and it’s not good.
On that note, for the fir st time in its entire history under a Māori ward —125 years, I
think, of Nelson City Council—we’ve had a Māori councillor; after 125 years. But I’d also
like to come back to my first question, which was around the timing of someone who is
elected while their role is disestablished, and I’d very much like to hear the Minister’s
response. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I thank the member for
her questions. In regard to her first question around the timing, the bill is very clear. I’d
encourage her to read the provisions. Ultimately, the referendum takes place at the 2025
election but doesn’t take effect until 2028, as I explained before. Therefore, for those people
who are running in Māori wards, even if the public vote to disestablish it, that
disestablishment won’t take effect until 2028. If they win their seat, they will be duly elected
and they will have a role for that term of that council. Th e legislation is very clear. That
was the decision made by the Government in terms of the timing.
In terms of the requirements, we’ve already discussed this issue in terms of the
requirement for referendums for all positions or all types of ward arrangemen ts—which
is, effectively, what the member is advocating for. What the member forgets is that the
previous Government’s legislation took away from the public the ability—when councils
put in place Māori wards —to even go and make a complaint to the Local Gov ernment
Commission in relation to the distribution of the seats in terms of those wards. So there
was an unequal treatment under the previous Government’s position.
The position that this Government is taking is to reinstate the legislation as it was prior to
2021. It is to put in place the ability for the public to be able to petition where a council is
deciding to put in place wards based on whether or not there should be a Māori ward—rather
than it being around geographic boundaries. The public should have the ability to petition,
and then, if enough people sign that petition, for a referendum to take place on that.
For all other wards —whether it’s a rural ward; whether it’s urban boundaries —
ultimately, as councils go through those distributions, the public do have their say as well.
They are able to submit on those processes, and, if they don’t like what the council
determines, they can go to the Local Government Commission, who are the ones who
4666            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
have the final say. The council does not have the final say,  even in those wards. So that
is the position that we’re taking.
And those wards don’t differentiate based on which electoral roll you’re on. They are
geographical. They are based on your address.

items.speaker: CELIA WADE-BROWN
items.text: I’d like to follow up on this understanding of local
people having a say on local issues. First of all, I’d like the Minister to think about the depth
of a represe ntation review which goes into looking at not only equivalent numbers or
whether people are on the Māori roll or the general roll. I want to give you an illustration
from Wellington. It’s like Auckland: when most people think about Wellington, they
probably think about the waterfront. But, actually, we have a huge western hinterland —
now, of course, with kiwi in it. But what we discovered was that there were rarely people
from Mākara, in Ōhāriu Valley—and not the electorate—on the council. So we established,
we chose to have, in every representation review since, a Mākara Community Board and
an Ōhāriu Community Board. And for other somewhat historic reasons dating back to 1989,
we also had a Tawa Community Board.
Now, that’s the sort of complex decision-making—whether you agree in every case or
not, but it’s complex and it goes to the local people, and there were a lot of submissions
from Tawa and from the rural area. There is no way that you could get that information
in a binary referendum. And  for the record in this House, you can have a multi -option
referendum, which might be new to some. But we’re not looking at multi -option here.
We’re looking at whakaae or whakahē [agreement or disagreement].
Going on with the depths and the engagement and  going out to the wonderful
community halls that we have in the west of Wellington, as a select committee we
inquired and found out that councils were able, before making that decision in line with
this legislation as to whether to rescind the Māori ward, to establish one, or to have a poll,
that they could do consultation.

items.speaker: My question would really be
items.text: after this legislation has come into effect, what is the
Minister’s view about the time that a council would have to go out to their community, to
be able t o make a decision by 6 September? So if you walk that back, even with hard -
working council staff you really need to allow a couple of weeks or three weeks between
the end of submissions, and earlier if you’re also having hearings, which I think you should
on a matter like this. That actually means that if your decision making at the full council is
on 6 September, it goes to a committee a week before that, the report’s written before that,
and the hearings and the submissions are before that. Is 6 September  really fair if local
people are going to have a say on the matter that matters to them so much?
In all of the other important decisions that councils make: about how much they’ll spend
on wastewater or whether they will have a crossing, or whether they wi ll change speed
limits—if they’re still allowed to do such things—it’s taking time and connecting with the
community, rather than giving them a—we never had a referendum on 30 kilometres per
hour versus 50. We had evidence and submissions and discussion. A nd you can actually
weigh the evidence of whether it’s a road safety expert or whether it’s just somebody that’s
a little bit impatient and sometimes a little careless of others. And we could listen to that,
particularly when you were able to ask people in their oral submissions, which I think is
still—as we heard at the select committee—a great way of hearing from people.
So I would like to ask the Minister to give us his reflections on locals having a say on
the matters of elections and other council deci sions, how long that takes, and what kind
of consultation should be done before rescinding or proceeding with a Māori ward.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I thank Her Worship for
the question, and in answer to her question regarding consultation: yes, I acknowledge it’s a
short period of time. But, ultimately, we’ve well signalled the change. Some councils have
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4667
already started to have these conversations. F or example, Greater Wellington in their
submission even acknowledge that they are already having conversations with mana whenua,
and that was disclosed as part of their submission to the select committee.
In terms of her concern about making sure that the public have the opportunity to have
their say, I can allay those concerns by noting that they will have their opportunity to vote
in a referendum, and that means that everyone’s vote will count. It will count equally, and
they will be able to do that at the next local elections.

items.speaker: Hon KIERAN McANULTY
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. A number
of points I hope to make as the local government spokesperson for the Labour Party in
relation to the impact on local councils, the process of consultation, etc. However, I do
wish to speak to an amendment that I’ve made. I’ve submitted this because I was listening
very carefully to the Minister’s response earlier, I think it was to Rachel Boyack’s
contribution. Frankly, it was incredibly weak. He claims that there is a difference already,
previously, before the rules were changed, because they didn’t have the option to go to
the Local Government Commission, whereas all other wards would.
Well, just make that change. Just make Māori wards have the same process as the other
wards. Isn’t that your problem solved? Surely that’s a pragmatic solution. Then you
wouldn’t have to open yourself up to accusations of institutional racism and all the other
things that are going the Minister’s way—which, in my view, are founded.
The issue here is that I don’t think the Minister has actually fully discussed the
alternative here. If he really wants thing s to be fair, which was the guts of what he was
saying around the Local Government Commission —that there was a massive injustice,
so let’s throw the whole thing out —it doesn’t quite make sense. So if we really want
things to be fair and we want local commu nities to have a say, and if the Minister is
genuine in his distrust of local councils’ ability to make a decision for their communities,
let’s remove all decisions for all wards from councils.
I would encourage the committee to support my amendment which  will lead to that,
so all new urban wards and all rural wards and Māori wards would require a referendum
endorsing them from those communities. Surely that is the only fair way through this. We
could have avoided the whole thing if the Minister had just said, “Right, well, we’ve seen
an inequity here from their perspective that voters don’t have the opportunity to go
through the commission.” He could have changed that. And do you know what? I
probably would wager that we would have supported that, because it is fair across the
board, and that is the rationale behind this amendment.
Now, of course it does raise some serious issues around the process where Parliament is
being asked tonight—and will be if it passes tonight to the third reading —to essentially
remove democratically elected members. Now, this was alluded to earlier, but it’s
something that I think we should go into more detail. So for those councils that have already
decided for themselves that Māori wards are the right thing for them and their communities
and have had that in place at the previous local body elections like so many councils have,
they have a democratically elected councillor on their council that was elected through the
Māori ward.
If the member disputes that, I think he should loo k every single Māori electorate MP
in this House in the eye and tell them that he believes that they aren’t as equal as other
elected MPs, because if you can’t have one, you can’t have both. If you want to be a
consistent Minister, stand up and do that. I bet he doesn’t; he doesn’t have the guts. But
he’s quite happy to hide behind this.
We’ve got a scenario —and this is how it will play out if the Minister gets what he
wants—so you’ve got a democratically elected representative from the Māori wards in
these councils, this bill passes and the people that didn’t vote that democratically elected
4668            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
representative in have a say in whether they stay or go. How the hell is that democracy?
If he wants to be consistent, he should let the people that elected them decide , but no. I
tell you what, I would love a referendum to let the rest of the country decide whether
Simeon Brown should stay in the House. I would love that result. Would they stand for
that? Not a chance. Not a chance, because they wouldn’t like the result. What’s good for
the goose is good for the gander, and I’ve never seen a lack of a genuine, consistent
rationale as much as I’ve seen here. None of this stacks up, and if the Minister really
stands for democracy and really stands for consistency, he will support this bill, and I
urge the committee to do so.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Well, I’ve got news for
that member; I am supporting the bill, and so that’s just the first bit of news. The second
bit of news for the member: it’s hard to break it to him, but there was a referendum on
him in the Wairarapa, and there was one on me in Pakuranga on 14 October, so go back
and have a look at the numbers.
In terms of the question that was raised in regards to democratically elected members,
their positions being determined to no longer exist, that is not what this legislation is
doing. The legislation —any effect does not come into effect until the end of the te rm.
Either if they decide to rescind or to disestablish, the effect does not take place until the
next election. If there’s a referendum, the effect of that referendum does not take effect
till the next local election.
I just put it on the record of the House that no elected member has a right to a seat around
a council table or a seat in this House. The only people who determine whether we sit here,
or we sit around a council table or a local board table, are the voters. The voters determine
that, and so no democratically elected member will have their position disestablished. There
will be the roll or the ward, but those decisions —if the position is disestablished, that
happens at a local body election period, at which point people have to go out to the public
and ask them to re-elect them. If there is a disestablishment, there is nothing stopping that
individual from standing for the mayoralty or for the community board or for the council.
Likewise, if the public decide to retain the ward, those positions  will continue to stay in
existence and the people will be able to stand for those particular wards.

items.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Just wanting to pick up on the
discussion that we’ve been having in terms of representation reviews and the place with
the Māori wards, but also, I think maybe the missed opportunity to hear the heartbeat of
New Zealand, which was something that was shared by Pita Tipene, deputy chair of Ngāti
Hine and the chair of the Northland Regional Council Māori council working group. He
said that, actually, if we go out for referendum it will be the death star for Māori wards.
Because, again, as we’ve heard in t his House, if we allow the entire community to vote
on Māori wards, then we will get voted down. It’s the tyranny of the majority.
Now, the Government appears to think that this legislation does not undermine Te
Tiriti o Waitangi, despite the findings of a Waitangi Tribunal urgent hearing on the matter,
but aren’t you interested in equity and fairness for all? Because in reviewing Māori
representation across councils, it’s really hard for us. We’re not on the same level playing
field. We very rarely get Mā ori councillors in on the general wards in our areas —it’s
very, very hard. And I’ve stood in local government twice, unsuccessfully —no Māori
wards back then.
I want to explore the representation review because that function of council enables the
method of hui. It enables the opportunity for submissions. It enables surveys—a variety of
means to hear the voice of community. A referendum is a blunt tool. It is a blunt instrument
to thwack Māori over the head and knock us out, because, ultimately, if you really wanted
to hear the genuine voice of the people, you would sit in the community hall with those
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4669
grannies that turn up to every meeting, you’d send out the leaflets into the mailbox and
invite them to complete the QR code, click, fill out the survey—boom. You know, all of
the different mechanisms that councils use right now. And I must say, there are many more
ways to engage these days, and councils are doing a fabulous job. Then, a blunt instrument
of just one vote. Just one vote to people that may not hav e even engaged in the
conversation and who can fall victim to external forces, like Palmerston North where they
were inundated by Hobson’s Pledge, who came into the district and fuelled racial division
between Māori and tangata Tiriti. Our tauiwi Pākehā whānau.
Now, my question, in terms of the representation review, again, is that if we do go
forward and we have the referendum and we’re voted out for Māori—so as I’ve heard from
my learned colleague Rachel Boyack, she talked about actually the Māori is going to go,
and they’re going to campaign for next year’s local government elections, knowing that
actually you’re only going to get a three-year term because kua poroa te kaki—your head’s
chopped off. You’re only going to get three years, Māori mā. You’re only going to get your
three years, so make the most of it. This is just Māori straightness around, actually, what’s
the point? What’s the point for a Māori to stand knowing that a referendum has been held—
blunt instrument, boom! Kua mate te tūru, te wāri Māori. So why should our people bother
to stand? And it’s moumou. It’s really sad because, ultimately, Māori might work their
tero off—they might work their backside off—to prove their value in council from 2025 to
2028. Mō te koretaki noa iho—good for nothing—because, ultimately, the Māori will be
cut after 2028.

items.speaker: My question around it is this
items.text: if we are to have the death star, and Māori are going to
get the chop, our people vote in 2025 and say, “Na, poroa te kaki.”—chop it at the neck—
the Māori goes in and they spend three years proving themselves, does that mean that we
don’t get to participate in a representation review in six years’ time? Do Māori wards just
get the chop completely, or can councils come back in representation reviews and explore
Māori representation again six years down the line from 2025? That’s a question for the
Minister I’m really keen to understand, because we could mobilise again —community
voice—for this part of the representation review, or is it just done and dusted from the
referendum? Kia ora.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: Thank you very, very much Mr Chair. This is a
kaupapa dear to my heart, and from some of the speeches I saw this morning —I think I
called them ignorant and arrogant, because I saw this puffing out of the chest to put
something back to be what was right, which is consistent to what the Minister said
repeatedly this evening, that he’s put just putting it back to what it was. Can I encourage
some of my colleagues from the Māori Affairs Committee to stand up and ask some actual
questions of the Minister, given its significance to our portfolio, particularly after what we
saw on Monday? I was quite impressed with the Minister’s colleagues, actually, about the
empathy down in Kihikihi in the settlement that we saw there. But I’m not seeing the same
consistency in the House, and it sort of explains to me this Government’s position on
policies that impact on Māori—it’s semi-schizophrenic. However—

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: However, to the bill.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: I’m picking up at a point that the Hon Kieran McAnulty spoke
of, which is, sort of, the Minister knows best. There’s a low trust here of councils’
decision-making, and I just wonder, given that he is the Minister for Auckland as well, I
think, so he would have followed quite closely —and he mentioned the debate of the
potential establishment of Māori wards in Tāmaki Makaurau Auckland, I hope he
followed that debate, given it covers a number of his portfolios. I just wonder if he agrees
with the outcome of that decision from council —given that they didn’t move forward
with establishing Māori wards—and if he agrees with their reasons why, and, if it’s good
4670            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
for Auckland, given it’s consistent with his position on Māori wards, why he wouldn’t
offer the same confidence and trust in other councils like Gisborne, as an example? So
that’s my first round of questioning.
The second is around sort of a basis of evidence, because outside of the revenge politics
of this, I haven’t actually seen the Minister articulate his “why”. Why is this particular
piece of legislation, or putting something back, so right to him—

items.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson
items.text: He don’t like Māoris.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: Other than that, Willie Jackson. But his “why” has to have a
basis of evidence, I suspect. So from the submissions that he saw—

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I’ll just remind Mr Jackson, you don’t have to
use the “r-word” to actually be making comments that may be pushing you very close to
breach of the Standing Orders. Carry on.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: Going back to the question of evidence, and given that the
Minister likes to hear from people, I just wonder which submissions he actually listened
to that helped him form the argument to move this piece of legislation through. I had the
privilege of listening to a few submissions myself and they were quite different to what I
heard a couple of years ago. People have learnt quite a lot. The actual examples that we
had seen across Aotearoa New Zealand and in our councils, my sense, was that people
had lear nt quite a lot, that every Māori ward councillor that had been established
contributed heaps to council overall.

items.speaker: My question there for the Minister is
items.text: what evidence are you actually working on? Or
if this is just revenge politics, or if this is just institutional racism, then he should articulate
this evening—[Interruption] And, again, I hear a bit of noise over there —stand up and
ask your questions. Stand up and ask your questions Māori Affairs Committee, because
kua ngaro, kua ngaro [they’ve been lost, they’ve been lost].
Two questions that come in there around the Auckland Council decision on Māori
wards. Does he believe in that and how is that consistent with the position of other
councils that are quite keen to proceed with this? Secondly, please, pl ease, please could
he articulate the basis of evidence that has informed his decision to put this piece of
legislation through the House?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair.
and I just want to make a couple of comments about questions made earlier in relation to
the blunt instrument of a vote. Now, I’m not sure about what some members will think in
the House, but the criticising of democracy I find abhorrent. I actually think that allowing
the public to be able to vote is one of the most powerful mechanisms of consultation, and
that’s why we have democracy in New Zealand. We should be standing up for democracy,
not saying “times have changed”  and that we’re going to use QR codes to consult.
Actually, we believe in democracy and allowing the public to have their say. To be able
to tick a box and say what they think is ultimately something which should be respected,
which is what this bill does.
The second question in relation to Auckland —and of course I’m glad the members
opposite are being more enlightened and that Auckland didn’t have a referendum. They
voted as a council not to establish a Māori ward. They did go out for consultation. They
got views from the public. I think Cameron Brewer, the member for the great electorate
in the North, talked about the 68 percent of Aucklanders, he said. They listened through
that process, and of course the process under the new legislation would still allo w them
to go and consult. They would then be able to make a decision and if they do decide to
establish, then the people of Auckland would be able to petition, and if they receive 5
percent then there would be a referendum. If they don’t receive 5 percent, then that ward
would be established.
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4671
My views on what Auckland Council decided are actually irrelevant. They followed a
process. They got to the point in the process which they would still have to go through
under the law that we’re putting in place, and then they make a decision. Under this law,
if they decided to establish, then there would be the opportunity for people in Auckland
to be able to petition. If 5 percent of Aucklanders signed a petition, then there would be
a referendum of Aucklanders. If 4 .9 percent of Aucklanders sign a petition, there won’t
be a referendum and that ward will be established. But ultimately that is simply what the
process will be going forward. In terms of the issue—

items.speaker: Shanan Halbert
items.text: Why?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: In terms of why we’re doing this? Thank you for reminding
me. In terms of this, I mean, ultimately it comes back to democracy. The point that the
members forget is there was an election last year on 14 October and New Zealanders voted
for this coalition Government who campaigned on making these changes. We have been
elected to deliver on the promises we made to the people of New Zealand, and we are doing
just that.

items.speaker: DARLEEN TANA
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I actually look forward to the day when we
don’t need Māori wards and we don’t have to insist any more about he whakaputanga o
te Tiriti o Waitangi being somewhat like legal ob ligations or even aspirational, simply
because we are actually living into them and honouring them as we should. Aotearoa New
Zealand is home to two very distinct world views: one that is of the whenua that is for,
and driven by, the love for our mokopuna and the other is for the economy that is driven
for, and driven forward, by the love of money.
There was a time when I would have said that these two world views were not in
opposition, but that time has well and truly passed. Our local communities are und er the
hammer, and the means by which whānau can care for themselves are diminishing—

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Ms Tana, I remind you that we are talking about
the bill.

items.speaker: DARLEEN TANA
items.text: Yes, and I’m coming to that. Thank you, Mr Chair. But it’s clear,
to those of the whenua, that we need to pull more on the full remit of mātauranga Māori to
find responses to climate change and ecological collapse, which means that it’s not only
about having equitable governance arrangements, but it’s also about being essential.
I’m heartened by the pātai around the why of the change, and, indeed —given the
essential nature that we have Māori around the table at this time—whether the Government
would actually reconsider the amendm ent to include other wards in this consideration.
Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon Dr DUNCAN WEBB
items.text: Thank you, Mr
Chair—just a short point. It’s just referring to new section 19ZC, inserted by clause 7. The
question I have is about the eligibility of people to vote in the poll, because it’s always—
and it may be that this is a short answer and your officials will be able to whip over and
give you some advice. But I’m just looking and noting that the electors who vote in the poll
have to live within the rohe, within the territorial authority or the regional council area.
I’m just curious as to how that interfaces with what’s sometimes called the “landlord
roll”, and, in particular, whether a person who is a landlord and not a resident —doesn’t
actually live there but has a right to vote in a local body election by dint of being a
landlord—can have a say in the poll, or whether in fact you have to live there. It seems to
me that new section 19ZC suggests you’ve actually—it would be a good thing that you’ve
got to live within the constituency area to have a vote. So if you could just clarify that
landlords can’t vote on those matters just because they’re landlords and own rental
property in the area, that’d be great.
4672            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I appreciate the
opportunity for another call, because I did reflect on the Minister’s response to my earlier
questions and wanted to come back to him with some further comments and questions
because some of what he said didn’t quite stack up for me.
I will start with a contribution about the role that the Local Government Commission
play against the requirement for a referendum. The Minister commented, in response to
my question about other types of decisions made through a representation review —
so whether it be geographic, general wards, or potentially changing the voting system or
the number of councillors per ward, and those types of matters —he made the comment
that while those decisions don’t get the opportunity for a referendum, they instead would
go to the Local Government Commission.

items.speaker: I guess my question to the Minister is
items.text: if he was lo oking for consistency and fairness
around this process, wouldn’t he just put the Māori ward into a potential Local
Government Commission review framework as opposed to a referendum? What we now
have is an inconsistent approach to when the public may wish t o express dissatisfaction
with the decisions of the council. I do just want to point out to the Minister that, ultimately,
in those situations, it is actually the Local Government Commission’s decision; it doesn’t
come back to the electors. So if you’re go ing to make the argument that it’s about the
electors making that decision, actually it’s not; it’s the Local Government Commission
making the decision.
In the case of Nelson City Council, where I just talked to previously, there was an appeal
put to the Local Government Commission on the changes to STV and on the changes to
geographic and general wards. The Local Government Commission said, “No, we’re going
to agree with Nelson City Council, and the decision by Nelson City Council stands.” It
didn’t actually give a fulsome opportunity for the voting electors to actually have their say
on that. So I just wanted to put that to the Minister: why he’s not seeking to have consistency
across all of the different ways that you might challenge a decision of a council.
The second question I have, though, is based on—the Minister made a response earlier
around the referendum for Māori wards, that he’s returning the legislation to what it was
previously. Now, that’s actually not correct, and I’d like the Minister’s res ponse on this
because, under the previous form of the legislation, there was no automatic referendum,
there was no central government imposing of a referendum on local government; it
required a petition to be put forward, again by the electors of that constituency.
My question to the Minister, again, is: why—if he’s claiming to return to the previous
mechanisms through the legislation, I would put that that’s not correct, because he is
imposing and requiring all of those councils to have a referendum. But if he was actually
looking to return to what was in place prior, he would put back in place a petition process
for those wards that have been established. I accept that, going forward, anything that’s
changed post -legislation would come through the usual pe tition method in order to
achieve a referendum. I accept that. But we’re looking at those wards that have been put
in place since we had changed the law, as a Labour Government. Why has he not said,
for all of those wards, “In order to have a referendum, t here would need to be a petition,
and here is the time frame in which to do so.”, which is consistent with what the law was
in place previously? That would mean—

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Good point.

items.speaker: RACHEL BOYACK
items.text: I’ve still got a minute! So that would mean that he was actually
returning not only to the specifics of the law but the intent of the previous law. So those
are my questions to the Minister.
I do just want to speak very briefly, in my last remaining piece of my contribution, to
my colleague Kieran McAnulty’s proposed amendment, which, I think, would achieve
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4673
what we’re looking for, which is that consistency, which is that if you want the electors
to get their fulsome say, that’s fine, that’s the position of the Government. We don’t
necessarily agree with that position, in terms of a referendum approach, but that is the
position of the Government. Do it for all the wards. Do it for a geographic ward, for a
rural ward, for a general ward, for if there’s a decision made to have one at -large ward.
Do it for all of those decisions, so then we have that consistency and then we’re not in a
situation where we’re actually calling into question, I guess, the Government’s intent,
which gives me some concern on the basis of comments from Mr Halbert earlier. Thank
you, Mr Chair.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Oh, sorry, Minister, I missed you. I’ll leave it
with Mr Jackson—I’m sure he’ll provide you with plenty to answer.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: Thanks, Mr Chair. I just wanted to follow up on a couple
of areas in terms of evidence, in terms of the Māori view out there. I am interested in the
evidence because I was listening to the—

items.speaker: James Meager
items.text: Oh, turn the timer on—save us!

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: No, I will take time, thank you, Mr Meager—particularly
when you asked for me to take my time; I will do exactly that just for you.

items.speaker: James Meager
items.text: For the love of God, start the clock.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: But because I heard the Minister of Local Government—

items.speaker: James Meager
items.text: Time has stood still.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: —speaking earlier about consultation in terms of mana
whenua. We’re very interested, on this side of the House, on that and whether the Minister—
we know Mr Meager never talks to the mana whenua because he doesn’t know the meaning
of the word. But I’m interested to know if the Minister has actually had his own consultation
with mana whenua. This is on our consultation side, in terms of Part 1. Councils have done
it, but he has a relationship—I know he has his own relationships.
He was on council there with one of the Māori Party’s kaumātua Rangi McLean, who
he sets up as a bit of a good friend, which I believe he is. He’s also, unfortunately, a
member—no, no, he’s a member of Te Pāti Māori and he’s my cousin too, might I add.
So, I want to know, has he spoken to Rangi McLean? I’d like to know what did Rangi
McLean say to this Minister, who this Minister has said has played quite a major part in
his direction and influence. And is Rangi McLean ashamed of the Minister at this time?
I’m sure he would be, given the shocking legislation.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Mr Jackson, there’s nothing in the bill about
the likability of differing minds, so let’s just come to the bill.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: Well, can I come to new section 19ZA, inserted by clause 7,
in terms of the public notice of a right to demand a poll —which is, I think, particularly
important. Because we’re talking, in that regard, about what the process is —that’s what
Shanan Halbert asked—that the Minister went through in terms of determining his view
that this was the right thing to do, given his strong relationships—with Rangi McLean, for
example; incredible relationship he has there that he likes to talk about, but he certainly let
him down big-time with regards to that.
In terms of evidence, in Auckland, we’ve got a Māori statutory board, for example.
Now, this is a Māori statutory board that has been set up by the National Party and the
useless ACT Party. This is an ACT Party that ta lks about separate rights and they don’t
want division and everybody’s got to have one vote, and the ACT Party set up the Māori
statutory board. It’s a Māori statutory board that is working with mana whenua. It’s a
Māori statutory board that is working wit h people right across the board. It’s a Māori
statutory board that has been set up by this Government and their ACT partners. So where
4674            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
is the evidence to say that Māori seats can’t work, when you’ve got a Māori statutory
board in play right now set up by the ACT Party and the National Party?
I want to come to my learned comrade, friend, Kieran McAnulty’s question about
institutional racism, which the Minister has not answered. And it was put very early in the
debate. No, it was a question, and a relevant question, that the Minister has avoided
completely tonight. And I need to give him the definition of it because I’m sure, like his
friends over there, they don’t understand what institutional racism is. Also known as—this
is out of the Oxford Dictionary—systemic racism, it is defined as “policies and practices
that exist throughout a whole society or organisation that result in and support a continued
unfair advantage to some people and unfair or harmful treatment of others based on race or
ethnic group.” It manifests as discrimination in areas such as criminal justice, employment,
housing, healthcare, education, and political representation.

items.speaker: The question from Kieran McAnulty was
items.text: is this an example of institutional racism
where Māori are clearly being facto red out? There are separate rules for other groups
here: separate rules if you’re a property owner, separate rules if you’re if you’re in the
rural areas. Māori are being singled out. It was a relevant question from Kieran McAnulty,
and I want to know if the Minister has any understanding of what he’s doing in terms of
institutional racism, which is rampant, really, right across New Zealand society. In fact,
you could say that in every institute, in every area, in every part of New Zealand society,
institutional racism has been relevant. Does the Minister understand that at all?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I
thank the members for thei r questions. The questions in regard to the ratepayer roll
outlined in new section 19ZC, inserted by clause 7 —people in the ratepayer rolls are
entitled to sign those petitions.
In terms of the question around consultation, in terms of the policy, ultimat ely, we
took this policy to the election at the last election and New Zealanders voted for the parties
which now make up this Government and we are now implementing this legislation.

items.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson
items.text: Have you spoken to Rangi?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Well, that’s not relevant to the legislation. I speak to a lot
of people, but in terms of the specifics of the legislation, that’s not relevant to the
legislation. In terms of the wider point that’s been made about the policy intent and how
terrible it is, I would note it was the Labour Government which actually put these
provisions in place back in 2001. I’m not sure if the Hon Willie Jackson was a—oh yeah,
he wasn’t a member of the Labour Party then, was he? He wasn’t a member of the Labour
Party at that time, but those provisions were put in place then. We’re simply going back
to what the legislation was prior to the 2021 changes. We’re not even going back more
than 10 years in terms of the changes.
In terms of the question s around the pathway in terms of the requirement for the
referendum, there is a requirement for a referendum because there are a range of councils,
a number of councils, which put in place these wards where the public were not able to
have their say, and so we’ll be requiring them to either rescind or disestablish or to have a
referendum. Then, once that process is completed, councils will be able to put forward and
propose Māori wards. They will go through a consultation process, they’ll then be able to
make a decision, and then the public will have the opportunity to petition if they wish. So
if the petition receives over 5 percent of electors signing that petition, then there’ll be a
referendum at that point.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I’ll just indicate at this stage that standing up and
voicing opposition to the bill—the Chair will be looking for a little more than that.

items.speaker: Hon KIERAN McANULTY
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I appreciate
that guidance, as, I’m sure, so too does the committee. Whilst my intention was to respond
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4675
to some of the Minister’s comments, which in my view didn’t adequately answer the
questions posed, I will take that guidance and touch on a new area.
Now, this bill, in this part, touches obviously on referendum. It’s been discussed in
various details tonight, but what we haven’t touched on yet is the i mpact on councils.
Now, I’m sure the Minister has heard, as many members in this House would have heard,
local governments say that they can no longer absorb additional requirements without
assistance and funding. And that’s exactly what is proposed in thi s part and, indeed, the
bill more broadly—that is that the requirement on councils to hold referenda is a financial
implication on those councils.
With the reversal of the water reforms, the advice is really clear that the financial impact
on each council is significant, and we’re seeing that playing out already. There’s also been
a recent decision by the Minister to totally disregard, as a block, the recommendations from
the Future for Local Government Review. So, in that context, which is important for
people’s understanding as to how significant the financial cost on to councils could be, they
have no option but to increase rates now. There was the possibility that the Government
would explore alternatives, as the previous Government had committed to, but that’s gone
now—pretty much a couple of weeks ago.
Councils are sitting there with no other option but to increase rates. Now, councils are
financially strapped, and they are facing a situation where this Government —the Prime
Minister, the finance Minister, and the local government Minister himself—has basically
said, “They need to sort themselves out; we’re not going to help them.” The Prime Minister
is quoted as saying that local councils just need to stop doing dumb things, and the Minister
during scrutiny week agreed with him. How about the Government stops doing dumb
things? That’s going to help local government, because this requirement, as outlined in
Part 1, is going to require councils to pay for the referenda that they don’t want. Councils
have made it incredibly clear there are more councils opposed to this than there are councils
that support the Government’s alternative water reform, because they know it’s not going
to work and they know that this isn’t needed, because councils know that this is n’t
compulsory. Councils know they have the choice, and, indeed, councils have made the
choice that’s right for them. But what they don’t want and the choice that they haven’t made
is to hold these referendums.
The cost of this is actually quite significant. To provide context, there is a district council
in the South Island that has had to employ an additional cleaner to cover the public toilets,
such is the large number of tourists that their district attracts. Now, that additional cleaner has
meant an entire percent increase in rates—just to cover the cleaner. Now, that’s one person’s
salary, and it’s a 1 percent increase. So these are the margins that we’re talking about, with
local councils. Now, it’s quite clear to anybody that a referendum is going to cost more than
a cleaner. We’re talking, in some instances, a significant rates increase for something councils
haven’t asked for, which is actually an important question, I think. Perhaps someone else
might want to ask as to which councils—actually, bugger it, I’ll just ask you now. Which
councils have asked for this? I don’t think it’ll be any—not when it’s not compulsory. I think
it’s some small segment of National Party voters that don’t like the idea of Māori wards that
have asked for this. I don’t think it’s councils, but, certainly, the financial implications are
there. Does the Minister accept that this is going to cost particularly small rural councils quite
a bit, and, if so, why hasn’t he agreed to support them financially?

ngā kupu e whakakīnaki ai i tō tātou nei pāti.
[Thank you, Mr Chair; indeed greetings to all of us in the House. On my computer are

Those are the three representations that I have that I ha ve put as stickers because I’m
probably the only Gen Z in this whole Parliament—and the brother over there.

wards into the House many years ago.
4680            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
I wanted to actually quote from my submission that I made two years ago at the
Hamilton City Council pleading to councillors at that time to implement Māori wards.
Now we’re here in Parliament and they can potentially be removed or be put to a
referendum. My message at that time to those councillors —and, ironically, at that time

I think the reasoning for why I give this submission to the House is because it gives greater

was one of my questions to the Minister earlier on.
My message is “We are the first generation since raupatu to sp eak our language, to
attend wharekura. We have no choice but to be the first, and we will be the first generation
to speak in this council. So out of all cases you hear today, which one is going to make
us the first? Which one is going to matter 160 years from now so that our generations will

make sure that our voices never die out. We are here today to find a solution to the
problem and unite under Kīngitanga through kotahitangi.”
I ended my speech through this proverb from our Māori King “Taku kupu ki a koe,
Manuwhiri, kohikohia ngā maramara o te waka kia kōpū ki tō aroaro. Waiho mā waho hei
wherawhera; he kokopi kau tāu.”—“My advice to you, Manuwhiri, is to gather the remains
of our tribes before your presence. Let others divide them. Your task is to unite them.”  I
left with my statement, “Now where is my seat at this table.” I left the council demanding

Māori wards, from also MP for Hamilton—East or West?—

items.speaker: Hon Member

items.speaker: HANA-RAWHITI MAIPI -CLARKE

oppose this bill tonight.
Ironically, at the time, I vividly remember two years later we found a seat in Parliament.

The only Māori that are here are the ones making your cups of tea, the “dial-a-pōwhiri”, or

wards. There were so many other ethnicities on that council table at the time—Indian, South
African, Pākehā—which I though was absolutely beautiful, but nowhere to be seen was the
Treaty partner.
That’s what brings me to my question that I previously asked the Minister. When the
Government was formalised and officially became the Government of New Zealand, they
automatically assumed their obligation to the Treaty partner. So my question is: how does
the right of removing the Māori wards to local government representation constitute good
or appropriate Treaty partner behaviour within this bill? Tēnā rā tātou.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: The question is in
relation to the intent of the policy, and ultimately the intent of the policy is to allow councils
to be able to put forward recommendations. The public then are able to petition as to
whether or not there should be a referendum, and then the public get to have their say as to
whether or not the constitutional makeup of the el ectors of that council, and that ward
proposal, should go ahead or not. Ultimately, it’s about local people making decisions for
their local community and those local people being the voters in those electorates.
