simple—will the Minister consider a repeals process where, after the referendum, if there is
an unsatisfactory outcome or unsatisfactory process that’s been followed, will the Minister
consider putting a repeals process in this bill now, while we have the opportunity? And the
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4681
genesis of my question is, as I’ve looked through the Hansard, when this debate first
happened, the then Chris Luxon offered the same amendment. And now, sitting there in the
Prime Minister’s chair, I put to this Minister: will this Minister consider a proper appeals
process to make sure that if there is any undue influence or any undue happening through the
process of a referendum, whether or not there can be a repeal process put into the amendment
while it’s being considered now?
It’s a very straightforward question. It was one that was offered to this House when
this debate was first had by then Christopher Luxon, right now the Prime Minister of this
country—the Rt Hon Christopher Luxon—and whether or not the Minister will consider
this. It’s very straightforward. We’ve already heard a lot about how the referendum
process is—and I’ll use the words—the tyranny of the majority and it silences voices right
across the electorate, right across the country. And it’s not just Māori—it isn’t just Māori.
The tyranny of the majority does not just impact Māori; it impacts a lot of whānau, a lot
of community groups, rural groups, and others throughout the country. So with that in
mind, it is a very straightforward question: will the Minister consider a strong and robust
repeals process that will allow any mishap through the referendum process to be
prosecuted through an appeals process, and is he open to having that amendment put into
the bill now?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I think the member is
confused in that the issue which was being raised by the now Prime Minister was in relation
to the last Government not allowing an appeals process for t he establishment of Māori
wards when councils were going through the establishment and setting up of wards and
doing distributions. Ultimately what we have here is a thing called democracy where the
public, if they petition and 5 percent of the population or more sign a petition, there will be
a referendum, and ultimately that is the ultimate appeal in that the public gets to—

items.speaker: Steve Abel
items.text: The majority—the majority.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: —have their say, and I hear the members opposite criticising
democracy. Democracy might not give us the outcome—well, we will respect the outcome
of each and every referendum. And in some councils that may mean there is a Māori ward;
in some councils that may mean there isn’t. Ultimately, on this side of the House, we will
respect those decisions.

items.speaker: Dr LAWRENCE XU -NAN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I have a number of
questions on Part 1 and I’ll start with the first one. First of all, I want to thank the Minister
for clarifying a previous question by the Hon Dr Duncan Webb around whether ratepayers
in the so-called “landlord roll” are able to vote on this. I think that clarification was really
important for the question I am going to be raising.
When we are looking at section 19ZB(3), in clause 7, it specifies the definition of
“specified number of electors”. Now, if I cross-reference this to section 19ZC(2), it says
that “An ele ctor may sign a demand and be treated as one of the specified number of
electors only if,”—and this goes to what the Minister has clarified already —"(a) in the
case of a territorial authority, the name of the elector appears on the electoral roll of the
territorial authority;”. I’m assuming this is the part where the Minister says that people
who are on the colloquially termed “landlord roll” are able to vote on this. Correct me if
I’m wrong.
But the question I have is about fees. In the case of a regional council, the name of the
elector appears on the electoral roll of a territorial authority and the electorate address is
shown on the roll within that region. Now, like the Minister, I also grew up in East
Auckland. I am from Tāmaki-makau-rau, Auckland, and so admit that I have not as great
an understanding when it comes to the regional council or the size of the regional council.
But in this particular case, can a person own two separate houses within the regional
4682            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
council and have one on them on the elector al roll of the territorial authority and the
second one an address that is also within that region?
That clarification will be quite important for multiple reasons. Firstly, I agree with
what the Minister is saying, that democracy here is crucial, and also  the Minister has
addressed multiple times that this is about hearing from local communities. But one could
argue, regardless of whether you look at subsection (2)(a) or (b) of section 19ZC, that
ratepayers and landlords who do not live in that local commu nity are anything but what
is defined as hearing from that local community.
The second part of this—and this is from the commentary on the bill; the report of the
Justice Committee. I draw your attention to page 6 around the consistency with New
Zealand’s international obligations. It says, “The DDS comments that the United Nations
Human Rights Committee has previously raised concerns about the representation of
Māori in local government,”. Hence we have the Māori wards. But there is another section
in there that says, “Article 25 recognises and protects the right of every citizen to take
part in the conduct of public affairs. Article 26 enshrines a right to equality before the
law.” Now, having one person being able to vote multiple times is very much the
definition of inequality in this case. We are in a democracy, like the Minister suggested,
but what we are seeing here is not a democracy but an oligarchy. The more you can own,
the more money you have, the more you have a say.
That brings me to my final question on this particular section. Unless it is defined under
the original Local Electoral Act, section 9, which is about holding a referendum, which I
see in clause 5 of this Part 1, there is nothing I can see in Part 1 that specifies that a person
cannot put their name in more than once as part of a signatory to a demand.
Those are couple of questions to the Minister just to tie it all together. The first question
is, when it comes to section 19ZC(2)(b), when they’re talking about the scenario of being
on the electoral roll and having the elector’s address shown as in that, whether it could be
someone who owns two separate properties within the same regional council. And would
that, then, mean that a single person is able to put their name into the demand multiple
times, and is there any provision that bars or bans a person from putting in a name more
than once?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: The answer is that each
elector is only able to sign once.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. Thanks very much for giving
me another go to ask some questions of the Minister on this very important piece of
legislation that I can only see as actually taking New Zealand backwards and Māori
backwards. Again, I’ll go back to my colleagues in the Māori Affairs Committee—it would
be really good if you could make a contribution this evening. I would really appreciate
hearing your whakaaro on this. I think I saw the chair rise to his feet, but I think that was a
closure motion, not a question.
Minister, I have asked you, and other people have done follow-ups, about what evidence
you took on board to help make your decision in this sense. You haven’t been clear about
this yet. You haven’t spoken about the submissions that you really took on board,
particularly council views. And to come back to—I think there was a question around cost.
When I was sitting in submissions, I did ask around the costs of two councils for putting in
the referenda and the poll, and if we did that in Auckland Council as an example—because
it wasn’t that they didn’t want to ever do a Māori ward; it’s that they don’t want to do it
at this time.

items.speaker: My question for the Minister is
items.text: what in fact is the cost that he has considered that he’s
off-loading on to councils? Auckland Council, as one example, are on their knees financially
at the moment, and really struggling because of other decisions that he has made. What would
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4683
that cost be, Minister? Is he considering funding that cost to councils where they are in fact
following what will be his instruction through requirements of this legislation? Will he be
funding them to do that? And what considerations did he make, given that a decision for
council, if they wanted to continue a Māori ward, becomes a cost decision? If it’s going to
cost, for example, $50,000 to do a referen dum with your community, and your council,
effectively, is broke, then they would say, “No, they don’t want to pursue that.” So therefore,
that actually becomes a democratic barrier to a representation model.
I would appreciate if the Minister could articulate for me the basis of evidence. This is
my second time and I think the fifth time in the House that he’s been asked for any
evidence this evening. Minister, apart from your revenge politics that I believe I can only
see at the moment, what evidenc e is there? What are the costs that you’ve viewed and
taken on board? What are the costs specifically for Auckland if they want to establish
Māori wards in a number of years’ time—

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: No, they don’t.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: That’s not correct, Cameron Brewer.

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: Sixty-eight percent don’t.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: That is not correct. It’s about timing. And again, Cameron
Brewer, there you are, your arrogance and ignorance.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Please direct your comments to the Chair, Mr
Halbert.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: And it’s disappointing that still, given the sensitivity of this
particular—that it impacts Māori—that certain members of this House actually want to—

items.speaker: Cameron Brewer
items.text: You’re throwing the abuse, not me.

items.speaker: Hon Willie Jackson
items.text: You can handle it, Cam.

items.speaker: SHANAN HALBERT
items.text: Yeah, you’re a big boy. But the conversation here tonight
really comes back to my original question, which is what is the Minister’s why? And he
hasn’t articulated that. He hasn’t provided any evidence. He hasn’t spoken to any of the
submissions. He hasn’t spoken to the cost that he’s off-loading on to councils, how they’re
going to pay for it, or if he will fund it. So those are my questions for the Minister. It’d
be great to receive an answer. Again, I’d encourage my Māori Affairs Committee
members to make your contributions through questions this evening too.

items.speaker: HŪHANA LYNDON
items.text: Tēnā koe, Mr Chair. Mihi ana ki a koe. I want to
address with the Minister the binding poll component of the legislation, because I’ve just
been reviewing some of the advice that’s been received, and thinking about the New
Zealand Law Society and the way that they shared that “binding polls for Māori wards is
inconsistent with existing democratic decision -making frameworks.” Now, the bill
actually overrides the decisions of local government, and, actually, the ability for Māori
to determine whether they wa nt Māori wards or not would be a better solution. But, of
course, we’re asking all general “Joe Public” to make a decision around how Māori and
Māori on the electoral roll will be represented in local government.
In 2020, the Department of Internal Affairs  said, in their report, that binding poll
provisions had proved almost insurmountable as a barrier to Māori establishing Māori
wards and constituencies, because they raised in their report in 2020 that between 2002
and 2019, only two councils had established Māori wards via binding polls, seven council
resolutions were revoked via polls, and seven council-initiated polls were voted down. So
that leads to the question of why it needs to be binding, because, ultimately, referendums
can be a good mechanism to consult with your community, just like a hui. And there’s
provision within the legislation that other referendums can continue on their merry way.
But, for some reason, Māori get singled out again as the Te Tiriti partner who is relegated
to the back seat in local democracies and local government. And here we are, back to
4684            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
square one again, where “Joe Public”, at large, will have a say on how Māori voice is
represented in local government.
This is the New Zealand Law Society; this isn’t even the Waitangi Tribunal. We haven’t
even got into their report yet. But the law society said that the Government’s lack of
engagement with their Te Tiriti partners on this matter—because it’s affecting Māori in the
binding polls area—is actually one of the cruxes of the matters, and they recommended that
there needed to be a conversation before this legislation came into the House. Now, once a
Government is formed, it is bound by its commitments and obligations as the Crown to
Māori through Te Tiriti o Waitangi and should, therefore, follow—this is best practice—
policy development consultation processes which are consistent with the existing Te Tiriti
obligations and commitments.
Now, we know the Government did not talk to Māori before they brought it into the House,
and that’s one of the disappointing elements in terms of how you say that this legislation does
not undermine Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and yet they never considered talking to the Māori who
are the most affected by this. So my question to the Minister is around the binding polls and
why it has to be a binding poll on us. And, in fact, the referendum could actually be a really
good thing if it was to provide a litmus test and be one of the many mechanisms to test
where the community is at, generally; because, if I reflect on the select committee, those three
days of over 10,000 people who had provided written submissions and then came before us
over a three-day period after five days of space to actually submit our whakaaro—largely,
they all supported the retention of Māori wards.
So it’s peculiar that, actually, when it comes time for this legislation to come before the
House, our select committee voted us down, and yet the people of New Zealand spoke
really, really clearly that they supported —Tauiwi mai, Pākehā mai, o ur youth, and our
university students. I’m getting texts now saying, “Is it done? Is it over and out?” And I
said, “No, because we are here to fight for the retention of Māori wards as per the Te Tiriti
obligations of this Government.”  And, in fact, they are ignoring the advice of the New
Zealand Law Society. Let it be put on record that they are ignoring the advice. And I want
to explore with the Minister: why does it need to be a binding poll? Because, actually, the
referendum could be awesome as an enga gement tool, but, ultimately, it’s binding for
Māori, but it’s not binding for other things. Kia ora tātou.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair.
Well, I appreciate the member has gone from being opposed to the referendums and
saying that they are just a blunt vote to now at least an openness and a willingness to
explore them—so that is progress. But ultimately, this is about giving local communities
the ability to decide, and that is why we are requiring these to be referendums.
The list MP based somewhere in the North Shore, Shanan Halbert, his question was
around evidence. Look, I  mean, I have answered these questions multiple times this
afternoon in regards to the fact that on 14 October last year, the voters went to the polls.
They voted for parties which said they were going to change this law, we were elected,
and we’re deliver ing it. They might not like that, but ultimately that is democracy, and
we are delivering on what the public voted for us to do, and there are thousands of
submitters who made it very clear that they support this piece of legislation during the—
[Members seeking call]—I love the excitement—

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Let the Minister finish.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: —select committee.

items.speaker: Rawiri Waititi
items.text: Who’s running this Government?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I was just scratching my knee, actually, but I appreciate the
enthusiasm. As I said, there have been a range of comments and questions that I have
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4685
answered. Those issues have been well traversed during this debate and the answers
continue to stay the same.

items.speaker: DEBBIE NGAREWA-PACKER
items.text: Kia ora, thank you,
Mr Chair. I just want to make sure that anyone that may be offended by my tie puts some
sunglasses on right now. Just to progress with the questions, I am concerned, and Te Pāti
Māori does share, despite how we come across—we do have concerns for the relationship
of this Government with their tangata whenua. I guess we can see local government is
confronting enormous challenges—huge challenges—and you are denying yourself and,
indeed, Aotearoa opportunities.
The question I have is, if we look at the issues that are arisin g—the fact that we have
people who can’t afford rates, the fact that we have infrastructure needs, and we’re
consistently hearing from the other side of the Chamber about PPPs, which, in short, is
public-private partnerships. Those public-private partnerships are reliant on relationships
with iwi. So our question to the Minister of Local Government is—if we are taking such
“Well, iwi have a better economy than what we’ve seen in non-Māori”, and if you’re reliant
on, indeed, realising opportunities, as a chair of an investment subsidiary for iwi, I want to
know what you’re going to do to fix the relationship with Māori. Why would we do any
investment with Government when you are denying our rights as Māori, despite anyone
else that you have in local government? Why would I get involved, and why would our iwi
across the motu be supportive of infrastructure needs that you have—that you have?
I tell you now, you won’t be finding investments inside—the Minister won’t, I beg your
apologies. You will not be finding relationships anywhere else, from a PPP perspective.
How are you going to, I guess, unsettle the reputation that is coming out really loud and
clear, certainly in the other hat that I wear, that this is an anti -Māori, anti-progress, does
not want to do bus iness with iwi in an economic sense —what is the Minister going to
do, leading repeals like this, to address the relationship with iwi, to be able to sit down and
have opportunistic discussions about infrastructure and indeed the futuristic needs of
Aotearoa katoa?
I guess the other thing that I have to have, if in fact we are supporting local government’s
needs for wellbeing economically, environmentally, culturally, and socially —assuming
that we all agree on that—is how are you going to overcome this Government’s anti-Māori
reputation—by supporting, and in fact leading, this type of legislation—with iwi, the only
other investors that belong to this nation, that are going to be your biggest allies, should
they be allowed to?

items.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
items.text: Kia ora, Mr Chair. This is the first call I’ve actually
taken this evening on this legislation. I’d be interested to hear from the Minister and just
wanted to, I guess, have a bit of a reflection and then with some questions and maybe
some really amazing suggestions, which I’m sure he’ll take on board, because I know
he’s smart.
Evidence-wise, I just want to really reflect briefly, because it sort of keeps coming up and
up, and it’s one person, one vote—all that kind of narrative. Well, in New Plymouth, this
Parliament established the New Plymouth District Council in 1876, so it’s been around for
100—well, actually, up until 2019, it had been around for 143 years. Now, just evidence-
wise, we’ve only ever had two Māori elected members of council. The first one was in
1998. So it was 122 years before we got our first, and he was a rugby league star in New
Zealand, somebody—I’m not very good with sports, bu t anyway—Howie Tamati. Name
recognition; a good thing. He was the first. Then it was another 20 years until the second one.
Now, just for the record, for those two to be elected in the time of the New Plymouth District
Council, they are 0.43 percent—they are 0.43 percent of elected members, which is very,
4686            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
very small, I’m sure everyone in this committee can agree. Good people ran. Good Māori ran
for council—only 0.43 percent ever made it on to our council.
In terms of this legislation and in terms of this part of the bill we’re dissecting, I really
want to speak about the fact that times do change. The Minister has spoken several times
tonight. He’s spoken several times around the fact that, “Oh, the Labour Government put
this into law in 2001 and we threw this in, so get over yourselves. Stop being hypocrites.”
He didn’t use that word, because we’re not allowed to, but that’s the thing, right?

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
items.text: It was a bit squeaky.

items.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
items.text: It was a bit squeaky; exactly. Anyway, I just want to clarify. I just
want to, I guess, ask the Minister to think about this, and then I’ll go into the question
about it. It’s the fact that times are different in 2001. So times are different in, for example,
Taranaki. Times are different in the 1980s in Taranaki.
Now, Inglewood—I’m not sure if people know where Inglewood is. It’s an interesting
small town in Taranaki. They elected their first ever female mayor in 1986—the first and
only, actually. Now, the reason this is relevant to this legislation is because times change
and it moves on. So I reflect on 2001, the comments the Minister has made —that’s why
I mention this. The funny thing about that story —I know everyone’s gagging and so
interested—is that the mayor who lost hid t he mayoral chains, and they never found the
mayoral chains until he died. He hid them in this box —they actually had to make a
separate pair of mayoral chains, because no way were they having a woman mayor. How
dare they! The world’s going to implode and fall in; they have a woman mayor! So he hid
the mayoral chains. They had to create new mayoral chains —true story. Jenny Rowan:
she’s a good woman—a good elected member.
So what I’m talking about is the fact that —so I’m coming back to 2001, which the
Minister has spoken about at least three to four times this evening. He’s raised when we
bought this in in 2001. It was a different time back then and the fact is to get legislation
across, you have to—

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I’m just saying come to the bill.

items.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
items.text: Yep. I’m bringing it in with you there, Mr Chair. I’m coming in.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: People are enjoying your anecdotes, but—

items.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
items.text: So you had to do things as things will be done in 20 years’ time
and we’ll look back on them, and that is why we had that at that time. I remind you: 0.43
percent. So my question is—I’m just going to get to it now, because—

items.speaker: David MacLeod
items.text: Where’s David MacLeod?

items.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
items.text: Well, I don’t think you want to mention David MacLeod in this
committee, people, because he’s actually—

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Can we not refer to the absence of a member
from the Chamber.

items.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
items.text: I haven’t referred to the absence of a member; I was referring to
the member. If you want to look at in the media, potentially, the controversy is, people,
that he supports a Māori ward.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Let’s focus on the bill.

items.speaker: GLEN BENNETT
items.text: But anyway, just putting it on the Hansard there. It was in the
media last year. He supports a Māori ward. So my question is: when we look at the Local
Electoral Act 2001, which is part of this, so this is around how we, in Part 1 here, in terms
of referendum, I feel that we could actually remove the binding referendum out of this
legislation because —and I want some advice from officials, potentially, from the
Minister, because the Local Electoral Act 2001, if you look at section 19H, if you look at
19I of the Local Electoral Act 2001, they already have provisions for us to deal with the
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4687
fact of actual representation and reviewing that. So why don’t we just take thi s out and
go from there?

items.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. This is my first
opportunity to speak in this debate and I really appreciate the opportunity to take a call.
This will be a technical speech, and it introduces a new point that relates to new section
19Z(2), inserted by clause 6, and again further into the amendment that the Minister has
put forward at clause 7.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Section 19ZA, did you say?

items.speaker: ARENA WILLIAMS
items.text: New section 19Z(2). What I’m seeking to ask the Minister is,
essentially, a point about the consequences of those councils who have a large Māori
constituency creating a geographic ward to act as a de facto Māori ward.
Let me explain the context of this point, because it is a new point and I’d like to hear
from the Minister on it. Many councils around Aotearoa New Zealand have large Māori
populations—for example, the Rotorua Lakes Council or the Wairoa District Council. In
some of those areas, there are one or two geographic areas in the council’s boundary where
those areas are predominantly Māori. They have a population that is largely Māori and
where the other ethnic groups are minorities. Then there are some councils where if
geographic boundaries were redrawn where they have Māori constituencies currently, they
could use boundaries to define new areas.
What I’m asking is how the new provisions in section 19 impact on a council’s new
responsibility when it turns its mind under the new provisions to a boundary review. It
would be useful for the Minister, I guess, to take the committee through what those factors
are when a council will consider a boundaries review or a representation review under the
new mechanism, if they have Māori councillors sitting around the table, if they have a
new commitment to Māori representation in their councils, like many of the mayors who
have written to him have expressed that they do.
To give the committee some further context, there is a ticket that runs in the area that
both the Minister and I are from. It’s called the Action Team . When that ticket was first
established by the Hon George Hawkins, who was the Mayor for Manurewa later in his
life, but at the time he was Papakura Mayor, and before that a city councillor, my father
stood on that. It is also the ticket that the Minister stood on when he was elected to local
government. It has a proud history in South Auckland of representing the concerns of local
people. It is considered to be a highly localised ticket and it represents centrist views.
It’s important to recognise there that when my father was standing, he was one of the
first Māori to be seeking election in the area, in an area that had significant Māori
population. When he won that seat, he credited the Māori population in that area for
electing him. Later in his career , a representation review changed the boundaries. In his
view, the change of boundaries meant that he lost some of his traditional support base,
which was those Māori communities represented in that area.
I raise that question because that is a question which has been put to the Minister before.
He hasn’t had an opportunity to consider, really, the point that goes in the other direction.
If we have councils around the country who stand to lose their Māori councillors who they
have relationships with, who they have gained a lot of benefit from sitting around the table
not only in terms of their relationships with Māori communities but also their knowledge
of te taiao and their relationships with iwi Māori, which are both really important
considerations for local government representation, then are we setting up a situation for
ourselves where it is possible that councils around the country, particularly places like
Rotorua and Wairoa—I’d like an answer from the Minister on those two, particularly.
Will they be in a position where they will be trying to create constituencies of their Māori
voters in a geographic way, and does that create a situation where other people are not being
4688            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
represented in the same way? Would it not be better to have a Māori ward in tho se areas
where there is a high Māori population so that we can have Māori councillors who are
taking Māori views into account and representing Māori constituencies whilst also having
other representation around the table? Is it useful, I guess, to be using  the boundaries
reviews and the representation reviews in that way to now accommodate for something that
councils see themselves as losing? Are we getting ourselves into a situation where
representation reviews will be conducted up and down the country and result in something
like that which is not the intended consequence?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I thank the member for
her questions. The changes in the bill don’t affect how Māori wards are implemented, such
as the fair and effective representation arrangement rules. It is about whether or not
Māori wards are established at all and, obviously, the referendum arrangements. The issues
that she’s raising in relation to how those wards may be created—there is legislation and
are processes already in place, and there is the Local Government Commission, which,
ultimately, has the final say in terms of how those other wards may be created. Ultimately,
I reiterate the point that people who stand for election —if boundaries are changed,
ultimately, no one has a right to that particular electorate or council seat. It is the voters who
ultimately determine who wins.

items.speaker: Hon KIERAN McANULTY
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I’m still
waiting, actually, for answers to previous questions. One was in regard to the funding of
councils, particularly those that aren’t in a position to finance easily the costs of the
referenda, and that led to a subsequent question, which was which councils asked the
Minister for this. That’s actually an important one, because at a previous debate, when
we were discussing the proposed repeal of the water reform, I asked the Minister on
numerous occasions which councils did he engage with and he refused to answer. He
didn’t even get up and acknowledge it . I want to pre -empt that now and say we’ve seen
this trick before. I think the committee deserves an answer.
While he’s considering that, I am specifically considering here Amendment Paper 48,
in new section 19ZB(3). It mentions here —it defines—“‘specified number of electors’,
in relation to a territorial authority or regional council, means a number of electors equal
to or greater than 5 %”. Five percent is very low. I’m sitting there thinking about it. What
are the implications of 5 percent? First of all , it won’t require many people to bring
forward a referendum that isn’t broadly supported by the community. As the Minister has
said on numerous occasions—not necessarily in answer to the question, but nevertheless
it has been said—that is democracy playing out. But it also comes at a cost.
Now, if 5 percent of the population can trigger a referendum, that to me seems like
something that, really, councils are going to have to factor into their ongoing finances moving
forward. As I said earlier —and we might have been able to address this if the Minister
answered the question—small things, such as even just electing an additional cleaner, mean
a significant increase in rates for some councils. Now they’re potentially facing the costs of
a referendum that’s going to be triggered by 5 percent. It’s a reasonable question, and it’s not
one that’s been posed before, but would he consider increasing that?
If the referendum is going to be held and a majority needs to be sought in order to change
things, why trigger it  at such a low amount? When you consider a citizens initiated
referendum—even that’s higher, and that requires them to go across the whole country.
This requires them just to do it in a district. Now, as we know, some districts are quite small,
and it’s going to be very easy to trigger 5 percent. If all he wants to do is give people the
option to have a say—I don’t accept that, but this is what he said—5 percent is incredibly
low. Would he consider a different level? Would he actually engage with us on a proposed
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4689
amendment here? We can go away and draft it up pretty easily. Where’s the wriggle room
here? Five percent is very low—very low—so let’s work on this.
Ultimately, we haven’t had an opportunity, really, until now—until this committee of
the whole Hous e stage —to work our way through this Amendment Paper, which is
thicker than the original bill. We’re slowly going through it, and then we get to this. I did
put forward an amendment earlier, which he has indicated he’s not going to support —
which I think is a shame because it would actually achieve his pleas for consistency. So
work with us on this.

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Just to answer the
member’s questions in regards to funding, ultimately, there are a range of costs. Ultimately,
we as a Government decided to hold the referendums alongside the election to minimise
the costs.

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
items.text: It’s a bit of a cost though, isn’t it?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Democracy does have a cost. In terms of the 5 percent, that
is, effectively, going back to what the previous legislation was, which was put in place
by the Helen Clark Government. So we’re just simply putting that back in place.
In relation to the tabled amendment, he rightly points out the size of it. It makes one key
change, but ultimately that change has a range of tracked changes which are required
throughout the bill. But the simple change is it requires the council to make a resolution by
6 September whether to disestablish or rescind or have a referendum. So whilst, yes, it’s a
sizable document, ultimately there is only one change that is being made, effectively,
through that tabled amendment.

items.speaker: INGRID LEARY
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’ve got a little bit of a
different question, which relates to the d ata and evidence that is being relied on in this
bill. And I’d just hark back to the excellent visit that our caucus had to Tāmaki Makaurau
recently, and the presentation by Ngāti Whātua about Māori representation, but also Ngāti
Whātua representation and what many of us had assumed to be a citywide mana whenua,
which in fact was explained to us was quite different and was very much coalesced around
Ōrākei. And there were some explanations about how the representation in te ao Māori
worked, of where that mana came from and how that mana worked with those who either
whakapapa to Ōrākei or those who were visitors or those who came for a transient period
of time. I found it a really enlightening session.
When I look at this and the kōrero that they had around h ow that equates to a Māori
ward situation, and I look at the reliance of data and evidence based on Statistics New
Zealand, I’m really curious about what decision was made to rely on that evidence. I don’t
mean to be cynical, but we do know there were prob lems with Statistics New Zealand.
And we also know that Māori were a group that were very lowly represented in the data
that was given when it was collected in the previous census, and so, I would say, is
relatively unreliable and certainly from the representations made to us, and I do hope that
I’m not doing a disservice to those who represented, but my interpretation from Ngāti
Whātua was that this was a construct that was quite different, and the whakapapa has a
very different element to it.
I have a relatively short question for the Minister, actually, which is: what advice did
he receive and what thought did he give to ensure that Māori representation accords with
te ao Māori rather than just simply a sort of colonised view of things? And what has he
done to assure himself that the information that goes to and from Statistics New Zealand,
as I can see in Part 1 of the bill, and there is a requirement in both directions, as I
understand it —what assurance can he give and what assurances did he seek that th at
information and data set would be complete, that there would be trust in that from those
4690            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
who were contributing to it, and what assurance did he have that the representation from
te ao Māori perspective was going to be met by the bill as it’s currently drafted?

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I’m really disappointed
with the Minister’s responses tonight —particularly in the democracy area where he
waffles on about democracy, but no one can actually get a line on what the heck he’s
talking about in terms of democracy. It’s democracy according to the Minister.
I note that the former Minister of Education from National talked about democracy in a
lot of broad areas in the last couple of days and said that democracy was about diversity
and democracy was about treaties and democracy was about the Treaty of Waitangi. And
my good friend from Gisborne there, who knows Hekia Parata well, would agree with me
that democracy is more than just one person, one vote, which this Minister keeps waffling
on about but forgets that there’s lots of different examples, as Hekia Parata has said, of how
democracy has been tweaked and how it’s been changed. She’s particularly embarrassed
by this Minister and his nonsense about democracy, which brings us to just a couple of
areas that have not been addressed.
That’s why we want to support what Kieran McAnulty said—that the Minister does not
address our questions. I talked about institutional racism earlier and so did the Hon Kieran
McAnulty, and he hasn’t talked about it, hasn’t come back to it, doesn’t know anything
about it. I know he’s only about 21, but he doesn’t understand—

items.speaker: Hon Members
items.text: Oh, come on!

items.speaker: Rima Nakhle
items.text: Ageist.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: Well, I can’t help it if you put kids into these sorts of jobs,
but the reality is we want answers over what institutional racism is, and we’ve got nothing
from this Minister.
I want to also back up what’s been said in terms of new section 19ZB in terms of
“Electors may demand poll”: “(1) A specified number of electors of a territorial authority
or regional council may, at any time, demand that a poll be held on the question”—I think
this question’s already been put up, but, again, we don’t have the answer; this is 19ZB—
“…(a) in the case of a territorial authority, the district should be divided into 1 or more
Māori wards;”. The question here—and I think it’s b een well put—is that we’re talking
about a specified number of electors, but we’re only talking about 5 percent. That does not
at all fit the descriptions of democracy that the Minister keeps talking about. You know,
there’s this insistence that it’s about  one person, one vote, when clearly things have
changed. And I just need some clarification from the Minister with regards to this. In terms
of these electors demanding a poll, it seems that Māori —and we’ve been talking about
Māori all evening—don’t have the rights.

items.speaker: I also want to know from the Minister
items.text: if he does have any plans in replacing some of
the Māori expertise that are going to be removed from these boards, how do you replace
that expertise when you know that we’ve finally got access to democracy,  finally got
opportunities to getting on some of these boards? We have not had representation around
the country in terms of councils. That’s what’s driven this Act. It gave Māori an opportunity
to be on there. What’s the Minister’s plan in terms of replacing some of the expertise that’s
going off? You see, we have the Māori statutory board. You have all that expertise in
Auckland that the Auckland Council utilised. How many Māori have we got on Auckland
Council? One.

items.speaker: Hon Member
items.text: Three.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: Three. One and a half, I think. We’ve got a James Meager
type on there, too, I think.

items.speaker: James Meager
items.text: Aww.

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: I can’t help it if Mr Meager says he’s half a Māori. I can’t
help it if James Meager says he’s half a Māori; that’s his problem.

items.speaker: Rawiri Waititi
items.text: Yep. That was his own admission.
24 Jul 2024    Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 4691

items.speaker: Hon WILLIE JACKSON
items.text: That’s right. Not that I don’t respect James; I respect him
very much. But we’re talking about Māori representation here, and I’d like to know from
the Minister: how does he respond to that question in terms of electors demanding polls?
It’s a really relevant question. I’d also like him to come back in terms of institutional
racism. He still has not answered. That question was one of the first questions asked by
Kieran McAnulty in the debate tonight.

items.speaker: DANA KIRKPATRICK
items.text: I move, That debate on this
question now close.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: I will take some more calls, but I do want to
acknowledge that there has been new materia l that has been asked, and I do want to
acknowledge that. But there is also repetition.

items.speaker: FRANCISCO HERNANDEZ
items.text: Thank you, Mr Chair. I apologise if my
contribution is repetitive in nature—I only just got here, so I haven’t been following the
debate as closely as I could have. As I said, I only just got here. My question is around new
section 19ZC, inserted by clause 7, around the requirements for a valid demand.
Now, section 19Z(2)(d) says that “the address given by the elector who signed the
demand is confirmed by the Electoral Commission as the address at which the elector is
registered as a parliamentary elector and the addr ess (i) is, if the demand was given to a
territorial authority, within the district of the territorial authority; or (ii) is, if the demand
was delivered to a regional council, within the region of the regional council; or” —and
this is the crux of my question; it’s something that I’m really curious about, whether it’s
deliberately in there, kind of considering that the rationale for this is to increase
democracy—“(e) [is that] the elector has enrolled, or has been nominated, as a ratepayer
elector and is qualified to vote as a ratepayer elector in elections of the territorial authority
or, as the case may require, the regional council.”
My reading of this is that a ratepayer elector could actually demand a referendum in
an area that they might not actually live in. So is this actually democratic that some person
who just owns property, who’s on the ratepayer roll, essentially, is affecting the politics?
We already have heard some analysis, and I think there’s been discussion earlier, and
there’s been extensive critique of how the ratepayer roll—

items.speaker: Rawiri Waititi
items.text: Old McDonald had a farm.

items.speaker: FRANCISCO HERNANDEZ
items.text: Yes, yes. It’s fundamentally undemocratic. Yes, there
are lots of McDonald’s, you know. It’s really problematic if we ’re letting people on the
ratepayer rolls dictate and demand referendum—that’s problematic.
There was an excellent contribution by someone on the Labour benches that also talked
about the 5 percent requirement—I can’t quite remember who it was—but he mentioned
whether the Minister of Local Government had considered setting the threshold the same
as the citizens initiated referendum, which I believe is 10 percent. In my view, if it’s good
enough for having the threshold set at the citizens initiated referendum, it should also be
good enough to have that be the same in terms of having the specified number of electors.
It is really important that there is some consistency between the kinds of rules at the local
and the national level.
One of the questions that I also have is who is running these elections? Are these
elections being run locally by the election services—Electionz? We do know that, in the
local councils, they have quite terrible turnout, some because of the nature of the poll but
also because of th e lack of promotion and the lack of democracy investment that goes
into it. If we’re serious about actually investing in our democracy, and if we’re serious
about making sure that people are fully participating, I think there needs to be some level
of investment being made in our local councils so that they’re actually having robust
elections.
As other speakers have already said, councils are being squeezed around the country.
We’re seeing rates rises of 20 to 25 percent. Quite frankly, a lot of a lot of co uncils are
4692            Local Government (Electoral Legislation etc.) Amdt Bill 24 Jul 2024
struggling to afford just basic services and they’re getting a lot of complaints about the rate
rises. I just don’t see how in this era when we’re kind of already loading up councils with
so many demands—you know, we’ve cancelled the three waters, we’ve made them assume
control over the water services, we’re also shouldering them with the burden of climate
adaptation. I think it’s kind of consistent in that central government repeatedly loads local
councils, demands them to do things, but it doesn’t resource them to do so. I think this is
another example of how we’re requiring them to run quite complex elections, quite
expensive elections, and we really need to make sure that we’re resourcing them.

items.speaker: Just to reiterate
items.text: the ratepayer role, is that de liberate? I do find it quite problematic.
The 5 percent threshold —I think it should be raised to 10 percent. And also whether
there’s going to be more resourcing to local councils. Thank you.

items.speaker: Hon KIERAN McANULTY
items.text: Thank you very much, Mr Chair. I
acknowledge the guidance you gave the committee when you acknowledged it was new
material and gave the first friendly warning about repetition.
My question is a repeat, because the Minister hasn’t at all answered or addressed it. It
was a very simple question. It was the third time I’ve had to ask it. I asked him eight times
last time we were debating a local government bill, so I ’ll keep asking —what councils
asked for this bill?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: I have answ ered the
question in relation to why the Government has put this bill through. We are putting this
bill through because the public of New Zealand voted for this Government.

items.speaker: Hon Kieran McAnulty
items.text: How many councils?

items.speaker: Hon SIMEON BROWN
items.text: Now, the member there can keep asking questions; I have
answered the question and said that the democratic will of the New Zealand people on 14
October was a vote for this Government and we are passing this legislation. That is why
we’re bringing this: to ensure the democratic will of the public of New Zealand can be
had when it comes to establishing Māori wards.
The other question was in relation to statistics. The requirement for statistics is not
substantially altered by the bill. Curren tly, Statistics New Zealand provides statistical
information to support both parliamentary and council representation reviews under the
Local Electoral Act. The Government’s decision has to certify statistics used for
representation reviews.
The member who  resumed his seat from the Green Party earlier —Francisco
Hernandez—all of his questions or the points he made were already addressed in prior
parts of the debate, if he had been tuning in.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Members, the time has come for me to leave the
Chair and report progress.
Progress to be reported.
House resumed.

items.speaker: CHAIRPERSON
items.text: Mr Speaker, the committee has considered the
Local Government (Electoral Legislation and Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies)
Amendment Bill and reports progress. I move, That the report be adopted.
Motion agreed to.
Report adopted.

items.speaker: ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: The bill is set down for further
consideration in committee next sitting day. The House is adjourned until 2 p.m.
tomorrow. Goodnight, everyone.
The House adjourned at 9.56 p.m.

whakamoemiti atu mātou, mō ngā karakia kua waihotia mai ki runga i a mātou. Ka waiho

PETITIONS, PAPERS, SELECT COMMITTEE REPORTS, AND

ORAL QUESTIONS 
QUESTIONS TO MINISTERS 
Question No. 1—Police 
1. TANYA UNKOVICH (NZ First) to the Associate Minister of Police: What action 
is being taken to boost Police recruitment? 
Hon CASEY COSTELLO (Associate M inister of Police) : Last week, Police 
announced changes to their eligibility criteria, with individuals on their restricted driver’s 
licence and those holding a residence visa now allowed to start the recruitment process. 
These are examples of common-sense changes that will open the door for thousands more 
New Zealanders who want to serve their communities. 
Tanya Unkovich: Is the Minister aware of a noticeable response to these changes? 
Hon CASEY COSTELLO: Although it’s too early to claim victory, I can advise that 
over the last week, Police received 630 applications. 
Tanya Unkovich: Has the Minister received any other updates on recruitment and 
retention? 
Hon CASEY COSTELLO : I have been advised that Police are continuing their 
efforts to work closely alongside recruitment applicants to ensure that those who meet the 
required standards have the best possible chance of making it to the Royal New Zealand 
Police College (RNZPC). In terms of applicant numbers, I’m advised that in the first six 
months of 2024, Police have received an average of 526 applications per month. This is 
53 percent higher than the monthly average over 2023. Additional recruitment staff are 
4612 Oral Questions 24 Jul 2024 
 
currently in place and be ing hired to ensure that applicants can be processed, cared for, 
and supported as quickly as possible. Retention of staff also remains promising, with the 
average attrition rate— 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: They’re all going to Australia. 
Hon CASEY COSTELLO: Well, not according to the statistics over the last 12 months, 
at less than 5 percent. This rate is amongst the lowest of all employers in New Zealand. This 
Government believes the recent initiative announced by the commissioner to support front-
line policing, including setting up community beat teams and the focus on core policing that 
enables police officers to better focus on tasks that require their skills and experience, makes 
policing more attractive to current and prospective officers. 
Tanya Unkovich: Is the Minister aware of further plans to boost recruitment? 
Hon CASEY COSTELLO: Police continues to attract potential candidates through its 
online digital platforms, including the New Cops website and district recruitment activities 
and marketing activity. I’m advised that 10 of the 12 police districts currently have district 
recruitment leads in place who are working alongside the operational recruitment teams to 
deliver fitness, academic, and candidate support to both applicants and potential applicants. 
They also run localised events, including information evenings and community recruitment 
activities. I’m also aware that the community patrols have increased efforts to engage with 
ethnic communities on the opportunities available through a career in policing. Finally, to 
support further recruitment, I’m advised that a new highly visible recruitment campaign 
will be live within the next couple of weeks. 
Hon Ginny Andersen : How many additional police officers are there now in the 
police service since her Government took office? 
Hon CASEY COSTELLO : Police numbers have dropped since November 2023, but 
this was expected, with no recruit w ings commencing at RNZPC between October 2023 
and January 2024 due to the Christmas closedown period and the transition. Wing 376 will 
graduate next week on 1 August and a further wing will graduate every five weeks from 
then on. With 630 applications last week alone, Police are confident we can recruit sufficient 
numbers. 
Hon Ginny Andersen : Why isn’t the Government doing more to retain the police 
officers we currently have, given there are 124 fewer police officers since her Government 
took office? 
Hon CASEY COSTELLO: I’m glad the member asked that question. We are doing 
a lot. Firstly, we are investing in police being able to do what they do best, which is catch 
bad guys, and they are loving it. 
Question No. 2—Finance 
2. NANCY LU (National) to the Minister of Finance: How many people have used 
the Budget 2024 tax calculator? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance) : Since Budget day, when the 
Government announced its programme of tax relief, the Budget website has hosted a tax 
calculator. This calculator shows how much tax relief people will get based on their personal 
and family circumstances. It has been very popular. I am happy to tell members that the 
number of people using the tax calculator has recently reached half a million—to be precise, 
513,000 people have used the calculator to see what they will be getting in long overdue tax 
relief that the other side of the House voted against. [Interruption] 
Nancy Lu: Supplementary. 
SPEAKER: Wait. 
Nancy Lu: When will tax relief be delivered? 
24 Jul 2024 Oral Questions 4613 
 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS : Income tax relief will be delivered in one week’s time. 
Changes to personal income tax thresholds, the in -work tax credit, and the independent 
earner tax credit will apply from next Wednesday, 31 July. On top of those changes, the 
new FamilyBoost payment, which reimburses families for a portion of their early childhood 
education fees, was launched on 1 July. 
Nancy Lu: What are the different elements of tax relief? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS: From next Wednesday, personal income tax thresholds will 
rise from $14,000 to $15,600, from $48,000 to $53,500, and from $70,000 to $78,100. The 
effect of these increases —these long -overdue increases in thresholds —is to reduce a 
person’s income tax by up to $40 a fortnight. In additi on, the in-work tax credit, which 
helps support low to middle income working families with children will increase by $50 a 
fortnight; and eligibility for the independent earner tax credit, which is for people who don’t 
receive a benefit or Working for Fami lies, has been extended from $48,000 a year to 
$70,000 a year of income. Parties on this side of the House are backing the workers. 
Nancy Lu: How much will people get in tax relief? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS : That depends on a person ’s individual and family 
circumstances. These circumstances differ widely, which is the whole reason for the 
Budget tax calculator. I would encourage New Zealanders who haven’t already done so—
and half a million people already have—to go to budget.govt.nz and check out their own 
situation in the tax calculator. 
Question No. 3—Prime Minister 
3. Rt Hon CHRIS HIPKINS (Leader of the Opposition)  to the Prime Minister: 
Does he stand by all his Government’s statements and actions? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON (Prime Minister) : Yes, a nd especially our 
commitment to deliver tax relief to low and middle income working New Zealanders, which 
takes effect next week. It is not radical to believe that tax brackets should be adjusted 
periodically to reflect inflation, and, after 14 years, it’s great that we’re finally doing it. It’s 
practical, it’s fair, it’s affordable, and it’s common sense. And I’m proud that this 
Government will do exactly that on Wednesday next week, when tax brackets are adjusted 
for the first time in 14 years. For an ave rage income household, that means up to $102 a 
fortnight and an additional up to $150 a fortnight if they have young kids in childcare. And 
my message to the squeezed middle is this; it’s pretty simple: after years of struggling 
through more taxes, more spending, more inflation, this Government has your back. We’re 
lowering the cost of living. [Interruption] 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Why should New Zealanders have confidence— 
SPEAKER: Just hang on. Just give yourself the space to  ask it with the House 
respecting your question. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Why should New Zealanders have confidence in his 
Government’s commitment to increase the number of police by 500 sworn officers, when 
nearly a quarter of the way through the parliamentary term, police numbers have actually 
dropped by 124 during his tenure as Prime Minister? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : We have ambitious and aspirational goals. We 
are determined to lower crime in this country. You cannot have a huge increase in retail 
crime, a huge increase in ram raids, a huge increase in violent crime and gang membership, 
without more police. That’s what we’re doing. We’re going to get more police. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Has the number of people unemployed and on a jobseeker 
benefit increased or decreased since he became Prime Minister? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : It has increased, and it’s happened because the 
previous Government increased Government spending by 84 percent. It drove up domestic 
4614 Oral Questions 24 Jul 2024 
 
inflation. When that happens, it raises interest rates. That slowed the economy, and it’s risen 
to high levels of unemployment. This Government’s determined to kill inflation to get it 
under control. It’s great to see last week it’s at 3.3 percent. We expect interest rates to come 
down when we get it back in the band. That will grow the economy, and that will keep 
people in work. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Well, can he confirm that his Government’s decision to 
increase the cost of car registration, reintroduce prescription fees, scrap public transport 
subsidies for young people, scrap affordable water reforms and other changes that 
increase costs for Kiwis has actually added half a p ercent to inflation in the last quarter, 
meaning we would already be within the 1 to 3 percent target inflation range now if they 
hadn’t done those things? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Oh my goodness! These are crocodile tears, aren’t 
they? Aren’t they? I mean, I’ve described that member as the arsonist who lit the fire, shows 
back up at the scene of the crime, and then blames us and the fire brigade for putting it out. 
That’s exactly what’s happening here, sunshine. That’s a bit rich coming from you. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: They don’t like the facts. Has New Zealand’s as yet unfunded 
emissions reduction liability under the Paris Agreement increased or decreased since he 
became Prime Minister, and is it his Govern ment’s intention to purchase international 
carbon credits to offset any outstanding liabilities that aren’t met through domestic 
emissions reductions? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Well, I can tell you the best way to deal with that 
problem is actually to lower emissions, and that’s what we’re planning to do. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Point of order, Mr Speaker. There were two parts to the 
question. The Prime Minister didn’t address either of them. One was whether the emissions 
liability has increased or decreased, and the second was whether they’re going to offset that 
by buying international carbon credits. He didn’t answer either of those things. 
SPEAKER: Well, that might be how you’ve heard it. I heard t hat he said that the 
intention is to reduce carbon emissions. That would surely deal with both those parts, but, 
however, I’m sure the Prime Minister would be quite happy to say something more. 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Well, as I’ve said before, we’ve got a great plan 
to be able to lower climate emissions. It’s different from the previous administration’s 
plan, but that’s OK. We’re focused on delivering the ends; we’ll just do it a different way, 
a better way. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Point of order, Mr Speaker. I don’t think anybody watching 
that would be any the wiser as to whether or not emissions are going up or down under 
his Government, and whether or not they’re intending to purchase carbon credits 
internationally to offset those emissions. 
SPEAKER: Well, possibly because they would have struggled to hear what was said 
because of the amount of noise that was coming from the —[Interruption] Sorry, is the 
member wanting to argue with me? 
Hon Dr Megan Woods: No. 
SPEAKER: I’ll have to go back over the audio tape. I’m sure that the dulcet tones of 
the member will be very audible in that case. Ask the question again at no penalty and 
we’ll see what comes of that. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Has New Zealand’s as yet unfunded 
emissions reduction liability under the Paris Agreement increased or decreased since he 
became Prime Minister, and is it his Government’s intention to purchase i nternational 
carbon credits to offset any outstanding liabilities that aren’t met through domestic 
emissions reductions? 
24 Jul 2024 Oral Questions 4615 
 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : Our Government’s intention is to reduce 
emissions, and what we’re going to do is pass fast-track legislation. I think that was a genius 
idea by the gentleman at the back—David Parker—who actually should be the leader of the 
Labour Party because he actually is principled and he actually cares about something. Fast-
track legislation is the way in which we lower our emissions. I’d encourage that member to 
support us. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Point of order, Mr Speaker. Perhaps I could help the Prime 
Minister by seeking— 
SPEAKER: No—not by point of order. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: —leave for David Parker to provide an answer to the questions 
as he seems to know more about it than the Prime Minister does. 
SPEAKER: Well, you could, but you’re not going to. So another supplementary. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins : Does he stand by his statement that “what we’re doing on 
interest deductibility is making sure we lower you know, we … actually put downward 
pressure on rents for renters.”; if so, by how much have rents dropped across New Zealand 
since he became Prime Minister? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Well, what I can tell that member is, in the previous 
administration, rents went up $175 a week. What we are doing is making sure that we increase 
the supply of houses being built, the supply of rental properties being available, and the supply 
of social housing being available. If we can do that, we can put downward pressure on rents. 
We can make sure that people get affordable housing. 
Rt Hon Chris Hipkins: Which of the following best demonstrates his so-called laser-
like focus on outcomes: fewer police on the beat, more people unemployed, inflation 
staying higher for longer, increasing greenhouse gas emissions, or higher rents? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Again, it is rich taking a lecture from that member 
on outcomes—this was a Government that spent more money, hired more people, delivered 
worse outcomes completely. You can’t hide from that record. We’re determ ined; we 
publish it every quarter. We’re very transparent with the New Zealand people. We have a 
quarterly plan. We actually announce our scorecards. We announce our progress against 
our targets. We’re going to keep doing it. 
Hon Kieran McAnulty : Doesn’t like questions from him; doesn’t like questions 
from us. 
SPEAKER: When you’re ready. 
Hon Kieran McAnulty: Oh, can I keep going? 
SPEAKER: No, you can’t. 
Question No. 4—Prime Minister 
4. CHLÖE SWARBRICK (Co -Leader—Green) to the Prime Minister: Does he 
stand by his Government’s statements and actions? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON (Prime Minister): Yes, and especially the moves 
that we are making to deliver world -class infrastructure and to rebuild the New Zealand 
economy. We know the difference that world-class roads can make to local communities—
helping Kiwis move faster and supporting growth and investment across the country. So it 
was absolutely fantastic news yesterday that this Government is accelerating work on a 
four-lane expressway from Auckland to Whangārei as part of our hugely successful roads 
of national significance. We know the difference that roads like Waikato expressway and 
the Kāpiti expressway have made for the regions, and now we’re bringing that to Northland. 
Whether you’re driving an EV or a truck, running a business or going on holiday, great 
roads matter, and our coalition Government’s going to build them.  
4616 Oral Questions 24 Jul 2024 
 
Chlöe Swarbrick: Can the Prime Minister name just one policy in the Government’s 
draft emissions reduction plan that will “make it cheaper for households to reduce net 
emissions”? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : Well, what will happen is that we are going to 
double the amount of renewable energy in this country, and we’re going to  do that by 
accelerating our fast-track, one-stop shop legislation. I encourage that member to support it.  
Chlöe Swarbrick: Does the Prime Minister believe that our pathway to a climate -
friendly future lies in more extraction of coal, oil, and gas, or ensuring 100 percent 
renewable energy, or is he intent to keep talking out both sides of his mouth?  
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : What I’d say to you is that we are going to 
double the amount of renewable energy in this country. It is unacceptable to take eight 
years to consent a wind farm and then two years to build it. I would encourage that 
member and the Labour Party to actually support that legislation so we can get renewable 
projects consented in one year and built much quicker. I’d also say to that member, you’re 
well aware that under the ending of the oil and gas ban, we now have some energy security 
challenges around gas supply, and I’d encourage that member to also support that 
legislation too.  
SPEAKER: Before I call the member, I’d just say the little flick at the end of the last 
question could well see questions terminated in the future.  
Chlöe Swarbrick: Thank you, Mr Speaker. Does the Prime Minister know or care that 
if you add up the emissions reductions of his Government’s so-called key policies in the 
draft emissions reduction plan, they make up a third of the emis sions increase that his 
reversal of the oil and gas ban will create? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON : What I’d just say to that member is we are 
consulting on a draft emissions reduction plan. I encourage the New Zealand public to submit 
on it, and we’ll have a final plan announced at the end of the year.  
Chlöe Swarbrick: How does the Prime Minister feel knowing that his Government’s 
decision under even just the emissions reduction plan alone has taken us off track to meet 
our climate goals and will increase inequality? 
Rt Hon CHRISTOPHER LUXON: Well, we remain on track to deliver the emissions 
reductions budget one and emissions reduction budget two. 
Chlöe Swarbrick : Is the Prime Minister incapable or just too scared to answer a 
question, straight up?  
SPEAKER: That question is out of order.  
Question No. 5—Transport 
5. GRANT McCALLUM (National —Northland) to the Minister of Transport : 
What recent announcements has he made on the four -lane roads of national significance 
between Auckland and Northland? 
Hon SIMEON BROWN (Minister of Transport) : Thank you, Mr Speaker. 
Yesterday, I was pleased to announce that the coalition Government is accelerating work 
on the new four -lane expressway between Auckland and Whangārei. For t oo long, the 
lack of resilient transport connections between Northland and the rest of the country have 
been a handbrake on the regions’ economic development. Planning for a replacement to 
the Brynderwyns was abruptly stopped by the last Government and it’s left Northland far 
too often in a vulnerable disruption. That’s why we’re moving at pace to get this project 
back on track, and I acknowledge the New Zealand First - National coalition’s 
commitment to this project. 
Grant McCallum : How is  the Government accelerating work on these roads of 
national significance? 
24 Jul 2024 Oral Questions 4617 
 
Hon SIMEON BROWN: As part of our Roads of National Significance programme, we 
have agreed to an accelerated delivery model to deliver this project faster and more  
efficiently. Our accelerated delivery strategy includes a progressive public -private 
partnership model that will achieve efficiencies and innovation in planning, procurement, 
design, and construction across the entire roading corridor between Auckland and Whangārei. 
It will do this by treating the three roads of national significance as three stages of the same 
project and incentivising the partner to deliver excellence in design, construction, finance, 
maintenance, and operation for each phase of the expressway. This Government is focused 
on getting infrastructure built.  
Grant McCallum: What benefits will this accelerated delivery model have on these 
roads of national significance? 
Hon SIMEON BROWN : There is great news for the hard -working people of 
Northland. Our accelerated delivery model means the New Zealand Transport Agency will 
avoid multiple procurement processes and will deliver integrated design, construction, and 
maintenance operations across the entire Northla nd Expressway and allow greater 
efficiencies through scale to deliver the project up to 10 years faster than traditional 
processes. The coalition Government is delivering for Northland. 
Grant McCallum: What benefits will the Northland Expressway bring to Northland? 
Hon SIMEON BROWN: Well, once the Northland Expressway is completed, it will 
provide a modern, reliable, and efficient link between Northland and Auckland, unlocking 
economic growth and boosting productivity. La st year, a report by the New Zealand 
Institute of Economic Research found that the Warkworth to Wellsford section of the 
expressway alone would increase New Zealand’s annual GDP by $497 million including 
benefits for Northland. The AA has said, following this announcement, that this would be 
a “game changer” for Northland. Whangārei’s Mayor Vince Cocurullo has said it was 
awesome news and a project that “Northland welcomes with open arms”. 
Hon David Seymour: Does the Minister view this project as a cost to New Zealand 
or an investment in a region that has been underserved and called the “roadless north” 
for far too long, and, yet, has better weather, better beaches, and more potential to be a 
place and a hom e for more and more people for generations to come than perhaps any 
other region? 
Hon SIMEON BROWN: Oh, well, the fond remarks that man says of Northland are true 
for the hearts of many New Zealanders. But, ultimately, we know that if we want to unlock 
economic growth and productivity for New Zealand, we need to build the modern, reliable 
infrastructure that New Zealand needs, and that includes building the roading infrastructure 
that New Zealand needs. The last Government cancelled the Roads of National Significance 
programmes—one of the worst decisions they made. [Interruption] 
SPEAKER: That’s enough. Now we’re just going to try and have a degree of calm. 
The House is getting a little bit too fractious. 
Question No. 6—Finance 
6. Hon BARBARA EDMONDS (Labour—Mana) to the Minister of Finance: Does 
she stand by her statement that “The  Budget we delivered in May was a careful 
combination of investment in frontline services whilst also continuing to do our bit to 
keep inflation down”; if so, what specific initiative in her Budget, if any, can she point to 
that will reduce inflation? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS (Minister of Finance) : Yes. And to the second part, the 
member seems to fundamentally have a misunderstanding, because the significance of 
the impact of the Budget on inflation is not about individual initiatives but rather the 
overall impact of spending and revenue decisions taken together—for example, the more-
4618 Oral Questions 24 Jul 2024 
 
than-240 savings initiatives progressed by this Government in the Budget. I refer the 
member to Treasury’s analysis in the Budget Economic and Fiscal Update, which says—
and I quote —“The decisions taken through Budget 202 4 will on balance reduce the 
contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure.” 
Hon Barbara Edmonds: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 
2024 that will reduce rates that are up an average of 9.6 percent? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS : I can point to the fact that this is a Government that is 
spending wisely and that, therefore, the overall impact of our Budget is to reduce pressure 
on inflation. 
Hon Barbara Edmonds: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 
2024 that will reduce insurance that is up 14 percent, with some families paying an 
additional $2,000 per year or $45 per week extra? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS: Well, as with the answer to the previous question, I do not set 
rates, nor do I set insurance levies. And if the member thinks it would be appropriate for the 
Minister of Finance to set insurance levies, then there’s a much broader discussion we can 
have about that. However, what we are seeing across New Zealand is that many insurers are 
introducing risk-based pricing and are looking at the risks which exist in our insurance 
market. One of the most significant risks is the risk of climate change and the more extreme 
weather events that are created by it. A specific initiative in Budget 2024 is the establishment 
of the Regional Infrastructure Fund. And the first set of projects that that fund will support 
are flood-mitigation projects, including stop banks across our regions, which is intended to 
reduce the risk of major climatic events, which, in turn, will help the context in which 
insurance rates are set. And to the earlier question in terms of rates, again, we do not set rates, 
but we are a Government that is ensuring we are providi ng uplifts and support for local 
roading projects, for many of the projects that local government are trying to carry out, and 
we are supporting growth in our regions. 
Hon Barbara Edmonds: What specific initiative, if any, can she point to in Budget 2024 
that will reduce rents that are up 4.8 percent—and the medium rental is $600 a week? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS: I do think it’s important that the member continues to reflect 
on my answer to the first question, which is tha t we know the cumulative impact of the 
initiatives in Budget 2024, in Treasury’s advice, is to reduce inflation pressure. In answer to 
the question specifically about rents, I can tell you this: increasing costs on landlords through 
removing their interest deductibility increased pressure on rents. And so the corollary is this: 
in an environment where interest deductibility was not restored, I guarantee rents would have 
increased faster. 
Hon Barbara Edmonds: Why have rents increased by 4.8 percent when she said her 
$2.9 billion tax break for landlords would put “downward pressure on rents”? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS : As I just said, I am confident that it has put downward 
pressure relative to the alternative, which was ratcheting up costs on landlords. What that 
Government had budgeted for was to grossly increase costs on landlords, which, I believe, 
would have been passed on to tenants in the rents that were charged. But, furthermore, what 
we are doing as a Government is the most fundamental thing we can do, which is move our 
levers to increase housing supply. Ultimately, we want a situation where landlords are 
competing much more robustly in the rental market so that, actually, there is maximum 
downward pressure on rents, and that’s about fixing the Resource Management Act, it’s 
about fixing constraints on land supply, and it’s about the changes Chris Penk is making in 
the building and construction portfolio to make it cheaper to build a house. And I’ll tell you 
what we’re not doing: we’re not going around New Zealand promising people we’ll build 
100,000 KiwiBuild homes. 
24 Jul 2024 Oral Questions 4619 
 
Hon Barbara Edmonds: Will she continue to claim responsibility for the decrease in 
inflation, as set out in her media release last week,  when her actions have done nothing 
to cause it? 
Hon NICOLA WILLIS: I once again point the member to the Treasury analysis, an 
institution she used to speak very well of. The decisions taken through Budget 2024 will, 
on balance, reduce the contribution fiscal policy is making to inflation pressure. I would

10. CAMERON BREWER (National —Upper Harbour)  to the Minister for 
Building and Construction : What announcements has the Government made about 
remote inspections?

progressing work to require building consent authorities to use remote visual inspections 
as the default approach, so building a home in New Zealand can be easier and more 
affordable. It is an exercise in increasing productivity.

Hon CHRIS PENK: Well, a constant frustration getting in the way of those doing the 
building work is a cumbersome consenting system and an inconsistent one, including as  
to building inspections. Some councils typically conduct these in person, but others are 
much more forward-looking in using remote visual inspections. Where there are massive

in-person inspections?

TODD STEPHENSON (ACT): Thank you, Mr Speaker. I rise today to speak about a
